speechtext: Mr. MACDONELL moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 78) to amend the Railway Act. He said: This Bill is very similar to the one which I introduced last session concerning the issue by railway companies of what are known as commutation tickets or suburban mileage tickets. It is introduced now in order to simplify the law by removing obstacles that appear to exist to having this matter disposed of. The jurisdiction of the Railway Commission is not admitted m this matter, appeals having been taken from its ruling to the Supreme Court of Canada. The object is to put the issue of the commutation tickets under the same supervision as other tickets with regard to the obligation of the railway companies not to discriminate in their actions as against persons or localities.

I desire to ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) what truth there is in the statement which appeared in the ' Globe,' a couple of days ago that the government have practically adopted the principle of the Bill in regard to suburban service giving jurisdiction to the Railway Commission. This has been stated by the ' Globe ' editorially.
< GRAHAM. The facts as stated in the
Globe ' were new to me. I have not considered the matter since last session.
This progressive policy announced in the ' Globe ' may not be carried into effect?
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: CONDITIONS OF LIFE IN THE WESTERN PROVINCES.
speechtext:
LAKE (Qu'Appelle) moved the adjournment of the House. He said: The article to which I,wish to direct the attention of the House for a very few minutes is of an exceptionally scurrilous nature. It is published in a paper which claims a very large circulation in the United Kingdom-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
very nearly a million copies weekly-and that is my first reason for bringing it to the attention of the House. There are other reasons. One is that the editor, Mr. Horatio Bottomley, is a Liberal member of the British House of Commons, and his name appearing on the front page seems to lend some strength to the article as published in the paper. Also the article bears a name similar to that of a man well known in the world of art. The writer also is an artist: but evidently of a very different type from the other. The journal to which I refer is called ' John Bull,' and this is the article to w'hich I wish to call attention:

Further Warnings to Canadian Emigrants.
By Louis Wain.
Canada is at this moment making every endeavour to entice young able-bodied Englishmen to her dominions; her agents are scouring the country with specious promises and glowing reports, which are attracting young men by the thousands to try their luck in her western regions, which are nothing more or less than death traps for all but those who go out well provided for. Train-loads of raw lads, with from £10 to £100 in their pockets as their sole possession, and the barest of ordinary outfits, are being dumped into the western towns. In these towns they are compelled to stop until the snow and slush have disappeared, perhaps for a month or six weeks, or longer, the cost of living alone being six shillings a day. The majority get to the end of their resources before they can be moved to the particular claim district to which they are bound.
Once on the spot, their condition is pitiable in the extreme. Penniless, and without the means to move their small belongings, they have to scour a vast district in semi-starvation in search of work or for a likely claim. They are useless for skilled work, and so most homesteads pass them by.
Without Work or Money.
Being far from the beaten paths of civilized life, they meet with none but their own kind, and these, too, are poverty-stricken, broken-down, young-old men, who, if they have by chance survived the terrible rigours of one winter, have come out of it only at the expense of the stamina which goes to make a strong, healthy man. Utterly incapable of helping themselves, these poor wretches just keep life together until they have tramped to a chance charitable homestead, and if they have not the strength to work they may end existence in some lonely hollow, or at best make for the nearest township, there to lounge out a wretched, broken-down life until another winter relieves them of their sufferings. In most cases their hands have been so badly frost-bitten that they are quite incapable of undertaking any strong, manual labour at all. If he is very strong and willing to learn, he may perhaps be taken on at an existing homestead temporarily as an unskilled labourer, and so get through the summer months on four shillings a day and food and lodging of the roughest possible description, but the hard

work compels liim to spend his money in clothes, and the winter finds him in some township without the means to take him baok to the coast.
On the Trail.
But if he can find no work on the. old homesteads he must take his chance and strike one of the Indian trails-the only roads known in these tramping lake districts-and trust to luck. By chance he may happen upon a new homestead, one of the cheaply and hastily-constructed wooden shacks covered with earthen clods. It is evident that some poor creature has spent his summer in building his shack and in breaking up his IX out of his 160 acres of land-government requiring him to work on his claim for six months of every year for three years before it will grant him his free patent for freehold-that he has done very little towards preparing for the winter, and that he has kept alive only just so long as wood and food have lasted him, and then he has been frozen to death. Probably, as in hundreds of other cases, he has not had sufficient money to carry him through the winter, and had not the strength to walk through the snow even to the nearest homestead. The novice follows the trail again, sick at, heart, and comes upon a starving wolf snarling over a few human bones-the remains of another poor wretch who has been caught in the open in a powerless state, frost-bitten and paralysed by the intensity of the bitter wind and cold. Half a mile further lies another man's horse fallen by his cart, a pile of burnt-out straw by its side-the whole of the contents of the cart in fact-the man himself having been rescued earlier. Further on still he will see a riderless bullock wagon, the team still stiff with the frost, while a mile away is a rescue party bending over the remains of the owner of the wagon. He hastens to the spot and is glad of the bit of generous relief given by these kind men, a party of one of the many good-hearted efforts made after the winter is over, to visit the novice homesteads by the more matured and wealthy pioneer settlers, whose kindly aid just saves many lives in the nick of time. I
I do not think I need read much more, but there is one other paragraph which contains an .abominable attack upon the women of the west and so should toe brought to the attention of this House ; in fact it is this paragraph which has mainly induced me to bring this matter before the House. It is as follows :

This is hut a page of the whole story. If the country life claims its holocaust, the town life out west is little better. Western Canada is no place for the gentlewoman. The woman population is composed largely of half-castes, of a degenerate type, often redeemed women who have been sent out by rescue societies to fall back into a worse state than they were drawn from, and the lowest class of domestic servant who. if she is at all good-looking, soon falls away into wild life, for the girls are of too low a class for most of the men to
marry. The few better class women who do come out and marry, suffer and suffer badly from hardships which only the brawny, strong, animal type of countrywoman can stand.	.
There are, of course, many good women in the towns, hut they live in the midst of temptation, and are plagued by a class of men vulgarly nicknamed 'remittance men and their hangers on. These are men who receive monthly or quarterly remittances from distant relatives abroad. They crawl about with sunken heads, aged and careworn, more often than not just out of their teens; 'their Ians are covered up brothels, and officialdom winks.
I am an Englishman who settled in the Northwest between 27 and 28.years -ago, and I think I can claim some knowledge and some experience in reference to that country. I characterize the whole tenor of what I have read to this House are grossly malicious and untrue. Even in the very earliest days of settlement when conditions were much rougher than they are now, they .never were in the very slightest degree what has been depicted in that article. To one who is acquainted with the conditions of the country the article bears on its face the stamp of having been written by a man who is .absolutely ignorant of what he is writing .about, of a man who has never been in the country at all or who, if he has been in the country, is so ignorant that he has been unable to make himself acquainted with the conditions. The article is malicious especially with regard to its attack upon the female portion of the population. Speaking of the prairie provinces especially, over which I have travelled very frequently, and of which I claim to have the knowledge attained during more than a quarter of a century residence there, I confidently make the assertion that no more moral people exists on the whole face of the globe than the people of the Northwest. The phenomenal progress of the new provinces is in a very large degree due to the magnificent type of women whom we have in that country. It would be impossible for me to speak too highly of the immense help which they have given towards rendering that country what it is to-day. The article is a most cruel libel upon them and I conceive also that it is cruel to thousands of families in the old country who have sons or relatives out in the Northwest, that is if any of them are credulous enough to believe statements published in a newspaper of this character. Speaking of my own experience, I would say that compared with the .pioneer life of Which we read in the older days of the settlement of this country, pioneer life in the western provinces is merely childs play. There are practically no hardships out there, except such as a man makes for himself. When I arrived-.and the conditions are much the same to-day-I found the people hospitable to a degree, generous and kindJiearted,

' always ready with advice and assistance to new comers, always ready to welcome them, and to help them along, and there are thousands and thousands of people in that country who will bear (witness to the truth of what I say in that respect. Considering the number who have come out, the failures have been astonishingly rare. In practically every case of failure it is the man's own fault. The man who is willing to work cannot help but get on, and I know of no case where ia man willing to work has been unable to find work. That is a very astonishing statement to be able to make in regard to any country. We do not want the idle and shiftless ; the more idle (and Shiftless they are the more they abuse the country instead of abusing themselves, and I should be very much inclined to think that the basis of this article is to be found in the idle stories of some man who is of no use and who has been on that account unable to get along in the country. These idle and Shiftless men of Whom I speak are_ not the breed who made the British empire what it is to-day. The young man of spirit and energy Who is full of the colonizing genius which has made the British Empire, need have no fear in coming out to the western provinces of the Dominion and need not fear that he will not make a success of his life there.

I am not English-born (and that is nothing to boast of) but I have had quite an experience in that western country, and I believe I know the conditions there. I do not know anything about this man Wain, but I could express

my opinion of him in two words. However, as these words would be unparliamentary I shall have to content myself with thinking them rather than expressing them. The statements in this article are a gross libel on Canada and Canadians, and I think that the Minister of the Interior is the proper person to take steps to nullify whatever effect such scurrilous writing may have. There have been failures in the west as the result of inexperience. Twenty-five or thirty years ago the conditions in Manitoba were very similar to the present conditions in the further west, and for many years I have gone in and out amongst the people and I know them, and I know that although the great majority came here poorly off financially, yet they have been progressive and prosperous. It is the first time that I have ever heard or read of any question as to the morality of the women in that country. True, in the early days especially they underwent great hardships because they had not much of this world's goods, but they met their circumstances in a womanly way. On the face of this article, the writer shows that he does not know what he is talking about, and while in this country his statements will have no influence whatever, there is the danger that those who do not know us may take some heed in them. This House is right in making a strong protest.

I would not speak on this question were it not that there is in the article a reflection on the older provinces of Canada. According to the special census taken in 1906, out of 808,000 in that western country, 444,000 have come from the other provinces of the Dominion and 164,000 from the province of Ontario alone, so that any reflection on the people of the west is a reflection on the people of the older provinces. I shall not detain the House further than to say that the right hon. the Prime Minister, who has in his power the most effective means of reaching the people, should cause the strongest possible denial to be made of the statements that are to be found in this article. The people of the best families of our older provinces have gone into that western country to make homes for themselves, and they are aspersed in the most dastardly way by this writer who makes statements as false as they can possibly be. The effect of such writings may be to influence adversely towards Canada the very class of people we want to get into this country, and so the government should take the most effective means to counteract whatever ill effects such an article may have.

Mr. Speaker, I should noi have spoken on this question were it not for Mr. SCHAFFNER,
the means which have been employed to publish this libel upon Canadian resources and Canadian treatment of the immigration into this fair land. This man's writings characterize him as knowing nothing whatever of the subject on which he purports to write, but, we must remember that this article appears in a magazine, the editor of which is member of the Imperial parliament, a fact which is sufficient to stamp it with a certain authenticity when it goes into the hands of the million readers amongst whom it circulates. It is therefore inconceivable that an article of this nature published in such a magazine should pass unheeded by this House, and I am quite sure that no hon. member will grudge the time that has been taken in stigmatizing it as absolutely unjust and grossly untrue. In this same magazine I notice in the editorial column for which Horatio Bottomley, member of the Imperial parliament, is directly responsible, an article launched against Canada. What does the House think of this? I quote from the same magazine, of date December 10, page 919:-
It is the fashion just now for the Canadian papers to abuse this journal for its outspokenness in regard to emigration truths. The language of the gutter is the only argument they can find to refute our definite allegations-confirmed quotations from advertisements-that 'no Englishman need apply' for any job in the Dominion. An Ontario reader sends us cuttings from the Hamilton 'Spectator' (the first dated as recently as November 16th) with the remark that he has been over there more than seven years and does'nt know yet why Canadians are so prejudiced against Englishmen.
Under the heading 'It is'nt true,' appears the following:-'To settle an argument will you please state in the 'Spectator' if it is true that the gaols in England are freed of prisoners once a year and sent to Canada?' To this is attached the note, 'No.-Ed.' But in a subsequent issue 'Chirper' chimes in that he would Tike to add that possibly years ago such was the case, and the big majority^ of present day Canadians are the progeny of such scum.' I don't say this is a fact, but judging by the number I have met and worked with, I should think it is more than likely. How the Canadians do love the motherland.
That, Sir, is the work of a member of the Imperial House of Commons, and some definite action ought to be taken by the representatives of this government in England to make it impossible for a gentleman occupying so high a position in the councils of the empire to publish such a libel, or such a scurrilous article. With reference to the Englishman in Canada, I may say that 1 have the honour of being an Englishman myself, who came to Canada and found the conditions here to be such that any Englishman of energy, with any reasonable amount of ' get-up-and-get * in him, could

carve out a living for himself in this country, and receive all the encouragement possible from good Canadian citizens. There is everything in this country to encourage Englishmen of the right type to come here. Speaking for myself and for the class of Englishmen who have come to Canada and, as good, honest, intelligent, hard working citizens, are helping to build up the country, I say there is no country in the civilized world that offers better inducements to the Englishman who is not afraid of work, but who is prepared to meet the conditions and to wrest from them what this country has in store than this fair Dominion of Canada. I am glad my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle has referred to this article, and I sincerely hope that, with such means as are at the disposal of the government, libels of this character, unjust, untrue, and malicious in their nature, published and circulated as they are by so high an authority as a member of the imperial parliament, may in the future be prevented if it is possible to prevent them.

I feel, Sir, that I have a duty to perform in regard to this matter, if no other than to . disavow being classed among the broken-down young-old men who came from England and settled in Canada. I read this article in my shack in the west with the comfortable knowledge that I had plenty of beef, plenty of pork, and a good Dit of my own land around me, and a little bit of venison in the larder, shot strictly in season. I smiled and remarked to my family:
' It is astonishing what a lot of fools there are in the world.' I should have left the article at that. I do not think it is a wise thing to give such a stupid letter as the' one we are now commenting upon, the publicity and the comparative immortality that it gets by being placed on the pages of ' Hansard.' The press do not regard their emanations so seriously, so far as I have the honour of knowing them, on both sides of the Atlantic. They prepare each day's manna for each day's consumption, and then forget-why shouldn't we? That is the question I should have put to myself before taking the responsibility of bringing this matter before the House. I desire, of course, fully to associate myself, if it is necessary, in the condemnation of what has been very accurately described by my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) as_ a publication which bears the evidence of its being a lie on its face. But if it bears that evidence on its face, everybody will know it for a lie, and I cannot understand why it should be made the subject of comment in parliament. Mr. Bottomley is a very eccentric member of parliament, financier and journalist. He believes, like most British journalists, in the utmost freedom of the press, and it is a fine poim whether more harm will result from curtailing the utmost freedom of the press, or from the publication of an occasional lie. We all know that the lies in the press, whether in Britain or in Canada, are exceedingly rare, but they do appear occasionally. My belief is that the people in England who are kept from coming to Canada by such an article as this, are people who from their low order of intelligence are better left orit of the country. I have a much more serious purpose in rising to offer a few words on this subject; and, after all, Sir, there is a serious origin to this kind of writing in the old country. I am bound to do this justice to the press in Canada, that I have never read a word in the newspapers of Canada which for scurrility would compare with that letter. But there is a great deal of talk in private, and sometimes in public, in Canada which sets an example to journalists of the order of Mr. Bottomley.
' What is the price of Free Trade ? ' said Sir Joseph Lawrence at the Empire Club in Toronto on October 12 last. He answered in part, ' One million paupers.' He ought to have known, if he did not know, that he was talking nonsense. Seventeen out of every twenty of those paupers are either physically or mentally incapable of looking after themselves. I was a great many years ago medical officer to a parochial workhouse in the old country, and the paupers under my charge were almost to an individual either imbecile old women or old men who I knew had been drunken and improvident in their habits; and yet we have a member of the Unionist party coming and telling such a distinguished patriotic and imperialistic body as the Empire Club of Toronto that these imbeciles and drunken old men are the produce of Free Trade. Of my own knowledge they were born and lived a groat many years in Britain when she was under Protection, so that if they were produced by an imbecile system, it was Protection that produced them. I do not contend that for a moment, but I do contend that the responsible public man, and the responsible body of men who listened to him, who give publicity to a libel like that on England and England's fiscal system, are only traducing the old country in a degree somewhat minor to that in which this scurrilous writer traduced Canada. The tendency to preach the decadence of Britain we find occasionally indulged in for political reasons. On this subject I can do no better than quote the Hamilton 'Times' of October 24 last:
There lias been so much fool talk about ' British decadence,' that ignorant people even in Canada have come to think that, in spite of the evidence of the facts of British pros-

perity and progress, there must be something in it. We can hardly conceive of the unpatriotic conduct of the coterie of British partisans who conduct the campaign for protection and who stop at nothing, not even depreciation and defamation of their country, in the effort to forward their selfish and treasonous party ends. But among educated and intelligent people the cry of British decadence evokes only contempt for its makers. As Frederick Austin Ogg points out in the ' Review of Reviews,' the United Kingdom never possessed elements of strength equal to those of to-day. There is no question of decadence, save in the minds of a few defeated and discredited politicians, who, lacking an acceptable policy, and hungering for office, set out to attempt to lie ignorance into disquiet.	;	! . i* -If
I should like to repeat from my own knowledge that there is no country in the world where a man has to-day such opportunity to get on as he has in Canada. When I first came to Canada I did some of that early-morning lighting of the _ stove which evoked such expressions of pity from the Minister of Labour for the workmen engaged in that operation. I can only say that I have never been more conscious of any addition to the virility of my manhood than when going through that operation. When I had the honour of representing Canada a few years ago for immigration purposes, I told any Englishmen I met that if they wanted to pick up money in the streets they had better stay where they were, but that if they wanted to find a country where they would have the greatest scope for their capacity and vigour they should by all means come to Canada and that in this country, despite our protectionist policy, we looked upon immigrants who had a little money as a desirable addition to our population. There is an important political lesson in what has been drawn attention to this afternoon. What is that lesson? It is that after all the good sound old Liberal policy of each nation in the main minding its own business and attending to its own affairs is the only policy upon which you can build and maintain the permanence of the British Empire. Nothing could afford better evidence than this very discussion of the deep insight of that imperial statesman whom we all admire irrespective of parties, Sir Edward Grey, when he said that this attempt to draw closer the material bonds between the different portions of the empire will only lead to mutual recriminations which will in the end make, not for the good of the empire, but its destruction. That would be the lesson to be drawn from this whole business which would at all make it worth while bringing it to the attention of this House. I can only say in conclusion that I am proud to be a Canadian citizen, just as I am proud to be a citizen of the old country, and as we all are Mr. CLARK.
proud, I believe, to be citizens of the British Empire, and to look upon the old country as the head and origin of that empire.

It seems to be considered necessary by the Englishman in the House to-day that he should be the defender of this country against the writer of the scurrilous and untruthful article contributed to an important paper in the old country. The only disinclination I have to saying very much on this question arises from the fact that I do not attach any serious importance to this article at all. I read it for the first time last night, but having read the English press for some years and knowing what the English press has to say about Canada and Canadians every day, and when I remember that there are any number of English people in Canada who are in constant correspondence with their friends in the old country, I do not attach any serious importance to the article we are now discussing. I do not believe that it will affect one single individual on the other side. The people of the old country know the benefits and advantages of Canada almost as well as we do ourselves. The standing of Canada in the motherland to-day, the maintenance of that standing shown by the press of England, and the constant correspondence between the English people on the other side and this-all these make it impossible lor any single individual contributor to any newspaper to do any injury to this councrv by anything he may write. My hon. friend who brought forward this resolution, (Mr. Lake) suggested that the writer of this article might not have been in this country at all. I am rather inclined to disagree with him in that respect. After reading the article closely I am inclined to suspect that the writer has been in Canada some time and that he is one of these incapable, degenerate gentlemen who come out here and do not make good, and consequently had to make some excuse perhaps to his father for the constant remittances he was receiving to enable him to live. My impression of the writer of that article is that he belongs to that class who never succeed in any country. They come from every country and they all fail when they come to this country. But, as I have already said, the great majority of Englishmen who come here and whose success encourages their friends to follow are an object lesson that make it impossible for any newspaper article to have any detrimental effect on the English mind.

Before this debate is closed, I would like to say that I do not at all agree in the view expressed that this incident was not worth bringing to the attention of the House. While it is perfectly true that an article such as this

would be received on all sides in Canada with the contempt it deserves, I am not so sure that it might not have an effect elsewhere, and I say so for this reason. Coming from Nova Scotia during the Christmas holidays I met a very intelligent man, a Russian, who had been living some years in Canada. He had fought in the Russo-Japanese war and afterwards came to Canada where he had engaged in all kinds of work. He had been a teamster in railway construction and had worked his way up, and is now living in the city of Winnipeg and doing very well. I had not then seen the article in question, but after my return I found that it had been sent me by Mr. A. F. McLaren who formerly represented North Perth in this House. But this man with whom I had been conversing, and who had just come from Russia and Germany, told me that on all hands in those countries one saw translations of articles published in this very newspaper * John Bull,' describing conditions in Canada in the most com-temptible and untruthful way. It is perfectly time that such writings have no weight in Canada and it may be equally true that they have small weight in Great Britain, but I am not sure that they would not possibly have very considerable weight in some places on the continent, and I think it is only right that the truth should be told in this House in order that it may go out to the world. For my part, so far as the language of that article is concerned, it is simply a foul and contemptible libel. I cannot understand why it should have been published by any man who ought to know Canada as the man who is responsible for this publication should be in the position to know it. If he knows anything about this country, he must know that these words published in his newspaper are absolutely false and constitute a contemptible libel. I have no respect whatever for that freedom of the press which finds expression in the publication of that which the man responsible for the publication knows to be thoroughly and contemptibly false.
That is a freedom of the press for which I have no respect whatever, and I know that my hon. Mend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), has no respect for it either. It is just as well, it seems to me, that some notice should be taken of this; and I congratulate my hon. friend from Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Lake), for having brought the matter to the attention of this House. When it came to my attention I asked him to take this course as an Englishman who had lived for more than a quarter of a century in Canada, and knew, perhaps, as much about the opportunities that present themselves to any immigrant in this country as any other hon. gentleman in this House. So far as opportunity in
Canada is concerned, there can be no question. The wealth of opportunity that is before any man who comes into this country is greater than in any other country of the world at the present time. And, as has been well said in this House this afternon, any man of reasonable industry and capacity coming into Canada at the present time-and the same has been true for the past twenty-five years-is as sure of a comfortable livelihood as any man can be sure of anything in this world. So far as conditions in the west to-day are concerned, every one of us knows that they are infinitely easier-at least, I believe them to be infinitely easier-than the conditions that faced the pioneers in the maritime provinces, Quebec or Ontario, fifty or seventy-five years ago. I believe that there is no comparison. Any Englishman like the possible writer of this article, who is not able to withstand the comparatively trifling privations and hardships which face him at the present time, is a man of whom this country is well rid. And our duty is to expose in this House and everywhere abroad the absolute inaccuracy and falsehood of the statements which have been published in the newspaper referred to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There can be in this House but one feeling, and that is that we owe a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle for the action he has taken upon the present occasion. Not, I am sure, that the article to which he has called our attention, deserves any notice or that it is likely to have any influence in England or anywhere else. It is so false as to carry its own refutation. Yet the malice of it is so evident that it is well that it should be stigmatized as it has been by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle and those who followed him. These hon. gentlemen, my hon. friends from_ Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake), Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), Red Deer (Mr. Clark), and Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), are all Englishmen born who have made Canada their home, and whose character is well known, not only in this country, but also in the? land of their birth. If the article quoted, made any impression, the fact that these gentlemen are now members of this Canadian House of Commons and the statements they have made, must remove that impression.
Motion (Mr. Lake) to adjourn negatived.

subtopic: FRASER MILLS, BRITISH COLUMBIA, POST OFFICE.

speechtext:
* Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster) :
1.	Had the Post Office Department or any of its officers knowledge, at the time, that W. H. J. Robertson was transacting the busi-

ness of the Fraser Mills post office during February and May of this year?
2.	Was Robertson under bonds to secure the government and the public against loss from his operations?
3.	Who was the nominal postmaster, and
was he under bonds to secure the government and the public against loss through _ operations of himself, his employees or his substitute ?	-
4.	Has it been brought to the notice of the government that Robertson decamped with funds entrusted to him, under the supposition that they were being deposited with the post office, by workmen at the Fraser Mills, lately from Quebec, and unacquainted with local postal conditions?
5.	Has application been made to the government to reimburse' the persons so defrauded of their savings? If so, with what result?
6.	Has the department had information of the whereabouts of Robertson at any time since his disappearance? If so, has the department taken any steps to secure his return and prosecution?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FRASER MILLS, BRITISH COLUMBIA, POST OFFICE.
speechtext:
1, 2 and 3. At an office of the class of Fraser Mills the postmaster, in return for the usual commissions upon the legitimate business conducted, is required to provide reasonable post office accommodation, and to engage such assistants as may be necessary for the proper performance of postal business. Persons so engaged are employees of the postmaster, who is responsible to the department for affording an efficient service. In these circumstances the department had no knowledge that Mr. W. H. J. Resolved, that it is expedient (a) to regulate the manufacture, importation, storage, handling, testing and use of explosive material of every description; (b) to grant licenses to factories and magazines for the manufacture and storage of explosives and to provide for the inspection thereof and the payment of fees for such licenses; (c) to make inquiries into the cause of explosions, and of accidents caused by explosives; (d) to provide for tbe
appointment of inspectors and other officers required for tbe administration of the Act, and the payment of the salaries thereof; (e) to-authorize the Governor in Council to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the Act; and (f) to provide for the imposition, of penalties in contravention thereof.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is in Canada at present no law regulating the manufacture of explosives. In England, for a number of years they have had legislation regulating the manufacture and the use of explosives, and the effect of it has been to largely minimize the number of accidents in mines and on public works. It has become very apparent in Canada, that of recent years accidents are increasing from the-use of explosives on public works and in establishments which manufacture explosives. To demonstrate the necessity for ' a Bill of this kind, I will mention a number of accidents resulting from explosives during the last year, and some of which would in all -probability have been, if not altogether obviated, considerably minimized in their results, had legislation such as that now proposed been in force. In British Columbia in March last, an explosion occurred on Bowen island, resulting in five deaths. The accident occurred from using iron nails in packing dynamite and under strict regulations that practice would have been prohibited. On the Nar tional Transcontinental railway, in July last-, 400 pounds of dynamite exploded near La Tuque, resulting in five deaths and five or six persons being seriously injured. The statement was made at the time, that the workmen were endeavouring to open a can of powder with an axe, when it exploded and set off a long train of powder and dynamite. By the regulations to be provided under this legislation, the opening of cans of explosives with an axe or other iron implement will be prohibited. In May last, at Departure bay near Nanaimo, an explosion resulted in five deaths,
I think every workman in the factory at the time was killed. A quantity of nitroglycerine and acid was being brought from the main building into the separator when the latter building blew up, killing all the men in the vicinity. The conditions which existed in this factory at the time would not have been permitted, under strict regulations. At Sand Point, in July last, there was an explosion in a powder factory, which resulted in three deaths and five being seriously injured. No precaution had been taken in this factory to allow sufficient space between the factory buildings and under the proposed regulations it would not have been allowed to operate. Under the regulations contemplated, these factories will be licensed and the buildings must be erected with a view to their distance from roads and dwelling houses, as well as to the distance between the build-

ings themselves which form the factory. I have here a photograph of the Sand Point factory, and it shows six to eight buildings huddled together, all within two or three feet of each other. Such would not have been permitted in * any country where there was a law regulating the manufacture of explosives. Last summer a very serious accident occurred in the Hull factory, by which eight persons were killed and some twenty or thirty seriously injured. Under such regulations as we propose to make, this factory would not have been permitted to operate. We provide in this Bill that applications for factory or magazine licenses shall be made in such form and manner as may be prescribed by regulation, and the application shall be accompanied by:- (a) a plan drawn to scale of the proposed factory or magazine, and of the land and any buildings adjacent thereto, with the exact distance between the several buildings marked thereon.
At the inquest held on persons killed by this explosion it was given in evidence that there was only a distance of 24 feet between the storehouse and the house in which the detonators were kept, and only 15 feet between the latter and the magazine, and 20 feet between the magazine and the mixing house. Regulations governing distances between dangerous buildings will be issued under the proposed Bill, which will bring into force what is known in Great Britain as the distance tables. These tables show the distance which must be maintained between danger buildings in all factories. During a period of 30 years, since the introduction of this distance table in Great Britain, no member of the general public has been killed, and no dwelling house has sustained any serious structural damage by an explosion in any factory to which these distances apply. The Bill is a very short one. Under it authority is taken to make regulations. The Bill has been prepared upon the recommendations of Captain Des-borough, the chief inspector of explosives for Great Britain, who was invited by the Department of Mines to come to Canada to investigate the conditions here. He visited all the establishments for the manufacture of explosives in Canada. The Bill is very largely based on the English Act, which has been found to work very satisfactorily during the last thirty years, and we believe that under it the number of fatalities from explosives, where they are manufactured as well as where they are used on public works and in mines, will be very greatly reduced. When we get into committee on the Bill, I shall be glad to give full explanations of anything that 1 have omitted at the present time.
Resolution agreed to, reported, read the first and second time and concurred in.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister if it is the intention of the government to take a similar course with respect to this House. Has any invitation been received, and is it proposed to appoint a delegation composed of members from both sides of this House to represent Canada at the coronation ceremony?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have been informed that a committee of the House of Commons sent an invitation to some members of this parliament to attend the coronation ceremony. We have declared that if such an invitation came we would be very happy to act upon it. That was before the election in Great Britain. Since the election we have not received any other invitation, and I am not aware whether a committee of the new parliament has been formed to send such an invitation. I understand that the Australian parliament, whether on this invitation or not I do not know, have appointed a committee of members to attend the coronation.
Eighteen members.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Now that the election in England is over, probably the matter will be taken up, and we may receive a new invitation. At all events, it has not come yet, but whether the invita-tion'from the previous parliament continues or a new invitation comes, it is a matter with regard to which, so far as I am concerned, we shall be happy to place ourselves in the hands of the House. "

When the Postmaster General returns, he will have a report to give and also duties to attend to.

I understand that he was to sail on the 7th of this month, so that he should be here in a short time.

Public Buildings, N.S.-Halifax Citadel- new quarters for single men, $15,000.

This is a revote. The request has been before the department for some time. It was made by the Militia Department on December 22, i909. The appropriation was made last year, but no expenditure made to date and I am asking for a re vote. '

The minister will have, to take a little time on. this. We were not told yesterday that the estimates would come up, and we went away with the impression that government Bills would be taken up. That business seems to have slipped up as so much does in which the government is concerned, and now we are rushed into estimates. The Minister of Public Works will just have to exercise a little of that patience with which he is so largely endowed until we are notified that he is to be on the scene and ready for action.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, True, we did not mention the estimates yesterday, but the government measure which we were to discuss could not be gone on with owing to an objection raised by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden). I am not finding fault with his objection because I think it was well taken, but neither was it the fault of the minister in charge because he acted on the advice of the law clerk, who told him he could proceed in that form. We are, therefore, taking up the estimates, and I am sure that my hon. friend, who is always ready to help forward public business, will not persist in his objection.
But we are entitled to be ?iven fair notice as to what particular estimates are coming up.
I shall be glad to exercise the utmost patience and give my hon. friend all the information he may require.
Then give us a description of the Halifax citadel as a beginning.

As my hon. friend has visited the citadel frequently himself, I would not like to weary him and the House with unnecessary information. 1
i
may say that the re-vote we are asking is for the purpose of providing quarters for single men.
Are they a part of the naval brigade?
No, this is for the militia, and has been -asked for by the Militia Department.

How many men will
have quarters there?
I regret I cannot give that information.
We ought to know before passing t:iis item.

Which citadel dees this refer to? Is it the main citadel in the city of Halifax or the citadel in the main batteries on the arm? I have visited those citadels, and -as near as I can recollect, the citadel proper in Halifax contains a large number of quarters -not occupied. But there are new fortifications, and I would like to know whether this expenditure is to be on the old citadel, which is going into decay, or on the new?
As I understand it, there is only one citadel -at Halifax, and these barracks are built at the base of the citadel.
The main fortifications of Halifax are away out in the larbour.
That is not known as the citadel.

Not generally known to the public either, and the fortifications -all contain rooms and quarters for the men, and I cannot see how additional quarters can be placed in the old citadel without seriously destroying its value as a fortification. The hon. minister would expedite his items if he would give notice to members on this side when these items are coming up and keep faith with them.
For how many -men are these quarters and what kind of quarters are'they to be? Are they to be temporary >r permanent?
That is information which would be in the possession of the Militia Department, and I -am sorry my hon. colleague is not here.
Then this item had better be laid aside for the present and let us go on with other matters.

I am glad to meet the request of my hon. friend.
Halifax Dominion Building-Post office, repairs. i-c., $30,000.

This is for the purpose of completing the improvements. Provision was made at a previous session for the remodelling of the whole interior so as to make the building fire proof and fitted for post office purposes and for the Receiver General's office. The customs, customs warehouse and inland revenue offices were removed to the new customs building. The total cost of remodelling estimated at $147,038. The total expenditure from the 1st July, 1908, to September, 1910, $85,149. I assume that there will be a further expenditure to the 31st March of $32,347, and we are asking $30,000, which will no doubt complete the work.
When did the work begin?

Public advertisements were issued calling for tenders in 1908, and the tender of Mr. Keefe, which was the lowest, was accepted on the 29th June, 1908. The work no doubt began shortly fter. Supplementary tenders were called for the heating, elevators and fittings.
When will it be completed?
I cannot tell just now. That information will, I think, be found in an answer I gave before recess.

Are you going to spend $30,000 on it in the course of the approaching fiscal year? Apparently, it will not be finished until a year from now at the earliest, as I observed from what the minister has said that the amount expended during the current fiscal year will be about $32,000.
No, that is the amount which will be expended between the 30th September last and the close of the fiscal year.
What is the whole amount expended?
Up to September 30 last, the amount expended was $85,941.38, and the estimated expenditure between that time and the 31st March next is $32,848.

The work seems to have proceeded with no very extreme expedition. It has been in progress isince shortly after June 29,	1908, and
June 29, 1911, will still see a great deal of work to be done upon it apparently. Considering the public inconvenience which has been occasioned since the work has been in progress, it would seem very desirable that greater expedition should have been used. The minister (Mr. Pugs-ley), is aware of the conditions. While this building is being repaired, the Post Office staff has been accommodated, I Mr. PUGSLEY.	. S
think, in the new building, and the general post office is in the basement of that building, a very cramped and inconvenient place, as I have found in visiting the post office during the past year. There seems to be a good deal of dissatisfaction among the citizens of Halifax because of the lack of expedition in this work. In fact, if you ask them when the work is expected to be completed and normal conditions re-established, they will simply laugh and shrug their shoulders. Can the minister give an explanation why this work should have required a period of about three and a half or four years to complete?
It is not so long as that. The contract was let on June 29, 1908-two years ago last June.

I know; but, as I have said, on June 29, 1911, the work will not be nearly completed-probably it will take six months, or even longer, after that. So, I think I was strictly within the mark when I said that the work will have occupied three and a half years or more. That seems a very long time for a work of this kind, particularly in view of the public inconvenience occasioned while it is being proceeded with. I know the contractor, Mr. Keefe. He is a very good contractor, I think, but he does not seem to have put himself out to make haste in this particular case. Nor do the government seem to have taken any very energetic steps to hurry him up. Was any time limit set in the contract?
The minister said the work would cost $148,000. How is the difference made up between Mr. Keefe's contract of $94,000 and this sum ?

How much of that has been paid to the contractor?

The amount was $65,380, leaving to be paid when completed $29,703. The chief architect has ju&t informed me that he received to-day the final estimate of the contractor's work, so that that work is finished. All that remains to be done is to provide the post office fittings, elevator, ,electric fixtures, etc.
Is there any penalty in the contract for delay?
There is no penalty.

Is there any correspondence indicating the steps taken
by the government to expedite the contractor's work?

The chief architect tells me there is correspondence with the contractor calling his attention to the delay and urging the necessity of proceeding more rapidly. That is the nature of the correspondence.
It seems remarkable that a time limit should be fixed and no penalty for exceeding that limit inserted. Is it not unusual in government contracts to adopt that course?
No, that is the usual form of contract.
I thought a penalty was usually fixed for failure to complete in a given time.
Not in respect to public buildings.

What is the practice when the limit is exceeded? It seems to me the government are very much at the mercy of the contractors unless they propose to adopt the extreme course referred to by the minister of taking the work out of the contractor's hands. That is very often not a desirable course to take, but it is a good thing to have a penalty, even if you do not exact it, because the time limit is not of much service. The government, I suppose might claim damages for nonfulfilment, but in the case of a public building such as this, it would be difficult to maintain a claim for more than nominal damages.

Of course, we keep back a percentage on the progress estimates and then if there is undue delay we can say to the contractor that we will keep back a larger percentage, and in that way bring to bear a very powerful lever, the desire of the contractor to earn his money as soon as he can. Then, of course, there is the other course which we have sometimes adopted, of taking the work out of the hands of the contractor, holding back a certain amount of money, and calling for new tenders. Of course, we charge any additional cost of the work up to the contractor, but it has not been usual to insert a penalty clause charging so much each day. We have not had' many instances of great delay. In this case, no doubt, Mr. Keefe has been behind in his contract.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What was the chief architect's estimate for this work?
$165,000, but that is for everything. We are getting it done at very nearly $20,000 below the original estimate.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Have you an inspector on this work, and who is he?
Yes, he has been on it from the commencement to the present. He belongs to the chief architect's staff and his office is at Ottawa, and we sent him from Ottawa to inspect the work.
Have you a local inspector as well?
No, no local inspector.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is common report in Halifax that the post office fittings, letter boxes, &c., were bought some time ago, but that the contractor has been so long at the work that these boxes have got out of date, and that the department are buying new ones. Another report is that the fittings were not good enough for Jhe place. Is there any truth in that story?
The suggestion of my hen, friend is entirely new to the officers of the department. I cannot think that would be the case without their knowing it.
Is the contractor who is working on this building the same one who constructed the custom house in Halifax?
The same gentleman, yes.
Is the minister aware that the tile floor in the upper story of the custom house is afloat, that the tiles are loose and give out a hollow sound when walked on?
I am aware that there are some defects, but not that it is afloat.
That the tiles are loose and can be kicked around when a person walks?
I do not know that it is so bad as that.
I can tell the minister ficm my own experience that it- is.

I was very greatly dissatisfied; I do not hesitate to say so publicly, with the mode in which Mr. Keefe did the work in connection with the custom house in Halifax, and when the tenders were called for this building and it was found that Mr. Keefe's tender was the lowest it caused me a great deal of concern as to what steps I should take in view, of the dissatisfaction in connection with the erection of the custom house. But Mr. Keefe was the lowest tenderer, he is a reliable man, a man of means, an experienced contractor, and I do not see how I could justify a refusal to accept his tender, which was $20,000 less than the next tenderer. What I did was to exercise the utmost possible care in regard to this building; we sent an inspector belonging to the architect's staff at headquarters, and he has remained constantly on the work from that day to this.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have heard no dissatisfaction as to how the work is being performed on this building.
What was the cause of dissatisfaction on the custom house building?

I cannot give the details nowr, but I remember one in respect to the well of the elevator, which was not just exactly as it ought to have been, and the roof was not done to the satisfaction of the department; there were some leaks which we had to repair. Then there was the matter spoken of by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Jameson), as to the flooring in certain parts of the building. Altogether, the defects were not very numerous, but they wore annoying and afforded just ground for complaint against the contractor.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister speaks of his low tender. I know of a contract which was tendered for; the lowest tender was $60,000 and his was nearly $30,000 higher; so that, you cannot tell much about the figures of contracts.

I can give my hon. friend a more remarkable instance than that. A building costing about $250,000 was tendered for by three of the most reliable contractors in Canada and there was a difference of $70,000 between the lowest tender and the highest, but we gave the contract, as we always do, except for special reasons, wdiich must be reported to council, to the lowest tenderer.
Is it the practice of the department to get the estimate from their own officers as to what a building ought to cost?
That is always done.
Do you always let the work to the lowest tenderer?

We always let it to the lowest tenderer unless the tenderer happens to be a man of no experience in that particular work or unless there has been dissatisfaction with the mode in which he has performed previous work. In very few instances-there have been a very few instances since I have been minister-have we ever done otherwise than given the contract to the lowest tenderer. The reasons in those cases are presented to council and there would be no objection whatever to presenting the reasons to the House if they were asked for.
I had not in my mind any instance to give in which the successful tenderer was not the lowest.
If the hon. gentleman will give us such an instance

The minister does not understand me. I had not in my mind any fault finding in that regard, but what I want to know is if, in letting a contract to the lowest tenderer, you have any regard for the estimate of your officers. Supposing your officers reported that $60,000 was a fair sum to be expended on a public work and your lowest tender was $100,000, is it your practice to give the contract to the lowest tenderer without any reference to the value of the work when it is finished.

No, we always consider carefully the estimate of the chief architect. Sometimes, when the lowest tender is considerably higher than the estimate of the chief architect, we refer the matter back to the chief architect for his report and go carefully over his estimate. If he adheres to his estimate, in the great majority of cases we call for new tenders.
What value would you attach to that when it is quite evident that the estimate of your architect is exceeded from 25 to 100 per cent in the actual cost of these buildings?
That is not the case.
It is the case, and I can give you many instances to show that it is the case.
In this particular case the cost is about $20,000 less than the chief architect's estimate.
That stands out very noticeably as an exception.
No, my hon. friend is in error as to that..

If you take up the whole list of armouries from one end of the country to the other you will see that the actual cost, when the buildings are completed, runs from 25 to 75 per cent higher than the contract price, so that the estimated cost does not cut any figure at all.
My hon. friend is entirely in error as to that.
I will prove before you get through with your armoury estimates that I am not in error.
My hon. friend may take a ease here and there-

I will give dozens of cases.
Mr. PUGSLEY-where hundreds of buildings are erected dozens of cases would not be sufficient to establish what the hon. gentleman says.
I will give you three or four dozen cases.
It would keep you busy to do that.

I would like to ask the minister if the rule which he speaks of as giving the contract to the lowest tenderer with regard to the erection of public buildings also applies to dredging contracts carried out by the Department of Public Works?
Yes.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to a reply that he gave me before the recess. I was asking with regard to some dredging at Port Dalhousie, for the names of the tenderers, and so on. The contract was given to the highest instead of the lowest tenderer. There were two tenders from, I think, Ontario companies that were pretty much alike and very much lower than the tender of A. & R. Loggie, who got the contract. In that case certainly the minister did not award the contract to the lowest tenderer; in fact, there were two or three lower than the firm who got it. Of course, I will say that the minister did not award the contract at the price which A. & R. Loggie put in, but they gave them the work at very nearly the tender of some Eastern 'Construction Company. It was not carrying out the statement of the minister that he awards the contracts of his department to the lowest tenderer.
I am sorry that my hon. friend has not quite stated the whole truth. [DOT]
Pretty much of it, I think.
No, there is a very important part of the truth that my hon. friend has forgotten. He has not done it intentionally, but simply because of his having forgotten the facts.
Which part?

The part is this, that the lowest tenderer had other dredging work to do. That company had tendered for a number of different dredging works, it had not plant enough to put into this work and we awarded the contract to A. & R. Loggie at the price of the lowest tender, which they were willing to accept.
Very nearly at the lowest tender but not quite.
It was either identical with it or less.

The minister in that case makes himself the judge as to the ability of this company to do the work. If the company had not been able to do the work and had so much work that they could not attend to any more, they cer-

tainly would not have put in a tender, but, as a matter of fact, two of them did put in lower tenders and the minister in his reply said that, in his opinion, these tenderers, having as much work as the minister thought they could attend to, he gave the tender to somebody else.

My hon. friend has forgotten another matter. When we invite tenders we require the tenderer to specify the dredging plant which he has available for doing the work. When tenders are called for, the companies tender on different works and we know, because we had the evidence in the tenders of the companies themselves, that the lowest tenderers had no.t the plant which would enable them to do the work because they had been awarded other contracts on tenders received about the same time, and if we had not given the work to
A.	& R. Loggie we could not have had it done during last year. We said to A. & R. Loggie:	We cannot give you the whole
price of your tender, but if you are willing to take the work at the price of the lowest tenderer, as he is obliged to go elsewhere with his plant, we will give you the work and it was given to them at identically the figure of the lowest tenderer or at a less price.
I do not know that it is worth while to pursue this matter, as we are on public buildings, but I have the reply of the minister here.
I will be glad if my hon. friend will read it. What page is it?

Page 1102 of the Revised ' Hansard,' December 12. The General Construction and Dredging Company. Limited, offered to do the work, which is divided un into .three series, A, B and C; A at $8, B at $6, and C at 291 cents. The tender of the General Construction Company was: A, $2.65; B, 38 cents; C, 38 cents. Then came A. & R. Loggie, who offered to do A for $15. I presume that is $15 per cubic yard for solid rock, and $6 for boulders, and 441 cents for the ordinary spoil. The minister gave the work to A. & R. Loggie at $5 for A, which was solid rock, and he will notice that the General Construction Company offered to remove that for $2.65 per cubic yard. The minister in his answer does not say anything about B, -but he gives that for ordinary spoil, 291 cents. I have not had time to work it out. hut if it were worked out I think that Messrs. Loggie would not be the lowest tenderer.
The tender of the General Construction Company was for ordinary spoil 38 cents and for rock $2.65, but they had no plant capable of enabling them to drill rock. I do not wish to say anything
publicly against any contractors, but I may say they were entirely incapable of doing the work, and had no plant suitable for the purpose.
That was not stated in the answer of the minister. I presume each tenderer sent in deposit with his tender.

We require a certain amount for works in any one province. In dredging work it is very important to have a contracting firm that has done work satisfactorily in the past. If my hon. friend would make inquiry I believe he would not have given this work to the General Construction Company at any price.
Halifax Dominion Buildings-repairs, $4,000.
Will the flooring of the new customs house be repaired out of this vote?
Yes.
If the construction of that building was faulty in the way indicated, why is it not done at the expense of the contractor?

We did make the contractor do quite a number of improvements before we took the work off his hands, but the chief architect finally accepted the work and so far as he was concerned the work was closed.
Lunenburg Public Buildings-improvements, $800.
This is in connection with the clock on the tower of the public building and for wiring, and so on.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I thought the clock was settled for long ago?
This is a revote to finish the payment,
What is the total cost?
The tender was $1,600, and the total probable cost including wiring of the building, and everything complete, $2,900.
Was that work done by public competition?
No, we got prices from different people in the business.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Does the $800 include the fittings?
No.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It seems quite a price for wiring a building.
It includes what we call the fixtures for the electric lighting. The item is for the wiring of the building for electric lighting.
Was the clock bought by public competition?
No, prices were asked.
From whom?
Mr. Schultz was asked to furnish a price and it was acceptable to the chief architect who knows the value of clocks.
Who is Mr. Schultz?
A clock dealer in Halifax.
The minister does not adopt the policy of public competition?
Not in all cases.
Was there anybody else on the patronage list besides Mr. Schultz?
Quite a number.
Why did'nt you ask them for a price on this clock?

WTe selected a reliable man and asked him to furnish a price which I think my hon. friend will agree with me is reasonable. We desired to get a first-class clock and we dealt with a first-class man and got a good article.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There are other gentlemen in Halifax in the clock business who do a much larger business than Mr. Schultz. I might mention the name of Messrs. Brown & Company, but unfortunately Mr. Brown is a Conservative.
Why say unfortunately?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Because he could not get a chance to supply this clock.
Surely he would not weep over that, he probably had his turn.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And lie will have it soon again.
I don't know about that.
Who asked Mr. Schultz for a price?
The chief architect,
On whose authority?
On the authority of the minister.

Then we are to understand that the Minister of Public Works refuses to adopt the policy of public competition. I would have thought that an expenditure of $1,600 for a clock and $800 for wiring a building would be sufficient even in the eyes of the minister to call for public competition. I suppose the man who got the contract is not a clock maker himself, but a middleman.
ile is a dealer in clocks.
He is a middleman, you did not ask the manufacturer for his price?
The manufacturer is in England.

That makes no difference. The minister would not pass by a large dealer in Halifax, and go to a smaller one unless he had some reason. Am I right in saying that the reason was that Mr. Schultz is a supporter of the government?
The reason is that Mr. Schultz is a thoroughly reliable dealer in clocks. t
Are there no others?
Plenty of others.
What about that larger establishment in Halifax?
I have no doubt he is a good man. I have nothing to say against him.

I am talking about the principle. The hon. minister and some other members of the government say they have adopted the policy of public competition. When we point out that he purchases this clock from a friend of his for $1,600 and gives the wiring of the building to another friend for $800, the hon. minister, says these are reliable men, and for that reason they receive the contracts without competition. Why does not my hon. friend adopt either one policy or the other? Why would not a little competition in clocks be a gsod thing? My hon. friend stands guilty, because he walks past the largest clock establishment in Halifax, without even suggesting that its price should be asked, and gives the contract to a political supporter without any competition at all. When it suits my hon. friend's purpose, he adopts competition, and when it suits the party interested, he does the other thing. My hon. friend should go to the province of Ontario and see how governmeht business is conducted.
Legislating away* people's rights.
Whose rights were legislated away? Legislating in the interest of the people of Ontario to such an extent that your party has no life there at all.
I would be ashamed to be the father of legislation that is enacted in the provinces of Ontario.
What does my hon. friend refer to?

My hon. friend knows. Take the ease of the Florence Mining Company, whose property rights the legislature of Ontario took away and at the same time prevented them going into the courts. I would be ashamed to be the father of legislation of that character.
My hon. friend has not followed that case or he would know that the courts decided in favour of the legislation.
They decided that it was competent for the legislature to take away the rights of property, although they said that it was disgraceful legislation.

They made the
comment that even if the government of Ontario granted the fiat, they were justified in the action they did take.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must intervene. It is not relevant to an expenditure on a clock in the town of Lunenburg to discuss the legislation of the Ontario legislature.

I have some memory of this affair, and if the minister would like to have it discussed again, we will have it discussed, and I think we will convince him that his recollection of it is very much at fault.
Mr. Chairman, I regret the diversion, but I sometimes get sick and tired of the hon. member for Peel inviting us to look at the way they do things in Ontario.
May I be permitted to say that I think only on one occasion before in this House have I made such a suggestion.

I do not wonder at the hon. Minister of Public Works
geting sick at references to the administration of the province of Ontario because the contrast between that and the administration of this government is so startling.
Some things they do are startling.

For example, they keep within the estimates brought down to parliament, while this government
exceedis them two or three times over.
Mr.j PUGSLEY. For instance, the extensions to the parliament buildings 'in Toronto.
I have no knowledge of that. I was speaking of the Hydro-Electric Commission.

What does my hon. friend think of the action of the Ontario legislature in declaring that no man shall have a right to sue the Hydro-Electric Commission or the government for any damages that may be done to private property without the consent of the Attorney General ?

The minister
had better look at his own record. I myself brought to the attention of the House twenty cases of men who desired to present their claims to the Exchequer Court of Canada upon contracts entered into by Mr. PUGSLEY.
this government which were brought to an end by the Post Office Department. I pressed their claims in two or three sessions in this parliament, and the government from 1897 down to the present time has absolutely refused these men the right to prosecute their claims in the courts of this country. What does he think about the case of the men who own timber limits at Petawawa and who up to the present time have not been allowed any opportunity to press their claims.
What does the hon. gentleman think of it ?

I think that it does not lie in the mouth of the Minister of Public Works to say one word about it, and I think any man with less hardihood than he, would not venture to do it. It is a great compliment to his remarkable audacity that he should venture to do it.
Is that a parliamentary expression-audacity ?
It is perfectly parliamentary. If the Minister of Public Works did not. know that before, he knows it now.

Now, Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member had, to use his own expression, the audacity to make that statement with regard to myself, perhaps you would allow me to make a remark. What I say is that if the Crown unreasonably denies to an individual the light to go into court and claim compensation for damages which he sustains at the hands of the Crown, it is an outrage; and when the Ontario government asked the legislature of that province to take away the property of the Florence Mining Company and to declare that that company should not have the right to go into a court of law, I say that was an outrage which reflects upon the standing and the respectability of the legislature.
What about the Canada Life Bill?

The Canada Life Bill was different. It was simply confirming what all the parties interested had been doing for many years, and what they regarded as t.he rights of the respective parties. However, Mr. Chairman, perhaps we had better proceed with the clock at Lunenburg.
My hon. friend's supporters in the Ontario legislature never suggest or attempted to suggest anything like my hon. friend has said. They endorsed the government throughout.
I take exception absolutely to that statement, and I know.

So do I know. My hon. friend knows all about it until his party

was defeated in the Ontario legislature, but he does not know all about it since then because new methods have been adopted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the discussion has been allowed to continue longer than is proper, and I would ask the committee to resume consideration of the item.

We require some information about this clock matter. No doubt as election time approaches, there will be more clocks supplied. I would like to know what is the policy of the department with respect to purchasing clocks that cost $1,600. Is there to be a public competition or are government supporters to be selected and specially favoured?

The usual policy of the department is to call for tenders, but when we require a special kind of clock made by a special manufacturer the price of which we know, and where the cost is under $5,000, we might very well do just what we did in this case, and give the order to a reliable man to obtain the clock from England.
Does the minister know how much this clock would cost at the factory?
In England? The chief architect would have that information.

That is information which the committee ought to be given. Here is a clock which cost $1,600, not made in Canada, the minister said he knew the price, but now he tells us the chief architect would know. Why did the minister not buy direct instead of through some middleman and party supporter in Halifax?

The clock had to be installed by some competent man in this country, and we employed a reliable clock-dealer to purchase and install the clock. After recess, I will get the information from the chief architect.

Does the hon. minister intend going through the New Brunswick public buildings this evening? I ask because I unfortunately have an unavoidable engagement which would prevent my being here, and I would be much obliged to the minister if he would take up something else.

With the consent of the committee, I would agree that every opportunity be given my hon. friend to discuss the New Brunswick items on some other item. He does not, I presume, hope to prevent any of these items from passing.
No, but I desire to have information.
Let one item stand and the others can be discussed on that one.

That is objectionable because when a sub item is left, the resolution does not pass. But upon any of the Prince Edward Island items, or the British Columbia items, my hon. friend can discuss the New Brunswick items.
But the items having passed, I might not be able to get the information deshed.
I will undertake to give any information my hon. friend requires.
Might I ask the minister when he is going to have a decision on this question of the Hydro-Electric being permitted to connect its wires up in Toronto across the McGann property.

T have recommended to council that the works be approved of, subject to complying with certain conditions recommended by the engineers of the department.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I may say to my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) that I asked Mr. Ewart to look up the papers and get me information as to the cost of the clock n England. But Mr. Ewart has quite a distance to go to his dinner and then he would have to go to the office, so I am without the information at present. Would the hon. gentleman prefer to let this item stand, or allow it to pass with the understanding that the information will'be given later?
I am not particular.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As to the electric wiring, were tenders called for?
Mr. Ewart is getting information as to that as well.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Better let it stand.
Parrsboro public building, $15,000.
The site has been purchased and this is to erect the building.
Where is Parrsboro?
In the county of Cumberland. This amount is a re-vote.
What did the site cost?
It cost $3,000 and legal expenses of $28.25. The lot has three frontpages, respectively 69, 96 and 77 feet.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That seems a pretty good price for a lot in Parrsboro.
For so large a lot, well situated, I should not think it would be out of the way.
What is the size of Parrsboro?
In 1901, it was $2,700; pretty close on $3,000 now, no doubt.
That is an awful price for the lot in a town of that size.

I am sure if my hon.
friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) were here, he would take a different view.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We have to take advantage of his absence.
Who had charge of the purchase on behalf of the government?
I have not the name, but it was an official of the department.
Was the site purchased from the owner direct, or was there a mid-lemian?
There was no middleman.
Has the minister the particulars of the purchase before him?
