Only that the lot was purchased from Mrs. Vickery. Authority was given in 1908 for purchase at $3,000. Purchase was made on the recommendation of an official of the department and was completed through the Justice Department in the ordinary way.
Wolfville public building, $20,000.
Of this amount, $13,000 is a re-vote. Wolfville is a very fine town, the site of Acadia college. We have acquired a very good site.	s
What is the population of Wolfville?
About 1,500.
That is only a village.
It is more than that. It is an educational centre and well worthy of the building we propose to give it.
Has the site been purchased?
Yes.
What was paid for it?

It is an unusually fine site. The price was $4,000. There is a frontage on Main street of 171 feet with a width at the back of 197 feet, the depth on the east side is 212 feet and on the west side 220 feet-about an acre of land.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are the plans made for the building?
They are in course of preparation.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I suppose it will be the ordinary style of building, with accommodation for the custom house up-stairs.
Yes, and for inland revenue also.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In my own town, some of us are getting old, and we find it hard to climb the stairs. I should think that in Wolfville with such a large lot, it might be possible to have the custom house on the ground floor.
I do not think the people should complain at climbing one flight.
What will be the cost of the building?
The plans are not completed, but the idea is to erect a building that will cost about $30,000, not including the site.
What about a clock for this place?
I have not considered that subject. I regret to say the demand for clocks is increasing.
If the minister does decide to put in a clock, how will he go about it?
I should be guided by circumstances, and actuated by the sole desire to get a clock at the cheapest possible price.	.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When the minister is planning for the building, he should make provision for a clock. I should like to have a clock in the public building in my own town, Truro, but there is no place for it.

A good many of the buildings erected twenty years or so ago v'ere built with towers in which the opening was carefully left for the clock-face, but creeks were not put in, and now demands are being made upon me to fill these places.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister must remember that he belonged to the Conservative side of the House at that time and so was responsible.

I am glad my hon. friend has somebody upon whom to place responsibility.
Yarmouth public building, $2,500.

It is thought that this would be- sufficient to make the repairs needed in the Yarmouth public building, but since these estimates were made up it has been pressed upon out consideration by the member for Yarmouth that there

should he a very considerably greater addition to the public building there, and it is not impossible that, in the supplementary estimates I may ask for a larger appropriation. The accommodation afforded by this building is very limited, and the business is increasing rapidly. I think we shall have to give them a substantial addition instead of the comparatively small repairs that we proposed to make.
Will the minister go back and take up the Lunenburg item?
I think we had better pass that.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was asked to stand.
Better let it go through, with the understanding that the matter can be further discussed on some other item.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would sooner see it stand. We can take it up later in the evening, can't we?

Does the minister intend making provision for a public building at Weymouth? I do not see any item for Weymouth in the estimates, but there is need for a public building there. The post office and custom house are in two different buildings, both rented. The requirements of the place are such as to warrant a moderate expenditure for a public building to house both these offices as well as the inland revenue office. I submitted to the minister some data showing the revenues of the post office and customs house, and also the population to be served, and I hope the minister has given the matter some consideration. Perhaps he can say what conclusion he has reached.
I have not yet decided what will be done in regard to a public building at Weymouth.
When will the minister arrive at a decision?
That is a hard question to ask.
It is not a hard question to ask, although it may be hard to answer.
There aTe so many public buildings one cannot say when we will decide a certain matter.
Has the minister considered the matter at all yet?
I have thought of it, yes.
The minister seems to have derived a good deal of satisfaction from the thought he has bestowed on it, if one may judge from the merry twinkle in his eye.	*
There is more twinkle on the other side of the House.
If the minister visits Weymouth he will find there is a great necessity for such a building, and I hope he will give it his early consideration.
What is the population to be served?
The population to be served is about 1,500.
That would be more than the town of Weymouth, the town is smaller than that.
It is not an incorporated town.
It is a village.

Call it a village if you like, it is as well entitled to be called a town and deserves the consideration of the minister as well as these other towns to which he has alluded, and for which he has made provision. I register a request to that end now.
Prince Edward Island-Summerside armoury, $7,000.
This is a revote.
Have tenders been called for?
Under the vote of last year tenders were called for this building, and we are asking $7,000 to complete the contract.
Has the site been chosen?

Yes, and the contract let.
Tignish public building, $11,000.
What is the population of Tignish?

It is difficult to give the population, it is not an incorporated town but there is quite a large settlement which is known as Tignish, and which is quite an important place. The money orders issued last year were $16,953, and money orders paid $10,745.
What was the revenue?
Post office $988, and customs $2,141.
What is the population?
I have not the population. There are six stores, two canning factories, two hotels, two churches, a newspaper-it is a very thickly settled district.
It cannot be very thickly settled with a revenue of $980 in the post office. What will the building cost?
My idea would be about
What is the fact?
When I give an idea it may be taken as pretty nearly the fact.
The minister should tell us what he intends to spend here.
The instructions to the chief architect will be to erect a building not to exceed $15,000.
Have tenders been called?

Not yec.
_ Mr. STANFIELD. In what papers do you intend to advertise?
In a reasonably large number, sufficient to answer the purpose.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I notice that when some work was being done by another de-pai'tment at Truro tenders were advertised for in the New Glasgow and Halifax papers, although the work cost only a few thousand dollars, but not in the Truro ' Daily News,' a good independent paper which we have at Truro, with one of the largest circulations in the maritime provinces. I am only throwing out this suggestion in case a similar situation should arise in the minister's department.
New Brunswick-Campbellton public building, $30,000.
This is to take the place of the public building destroyed by the recent fire in Campbellton.
What is this building to cost?
The contract without the fittings is for $28,592.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You own the land?
Yes.
How long is the contractor given to complete the building?
Until December 25, 1911.
Is there any penalty?
No, there is no penalty clause.
Why not?
It has not been customary.

The minister must know that the government would get a great deal better work and their buildings would be erected in more reasonable time if they had Mr. PUGSLEY.
a penalty. I cannot understand why the government should not insert a penalty of so much per day as other people do, and I would like to know why It was thought best not to. do this?

The reason is that it has not been found, except in rare instances, that there has been any public inconvenience caused by delays of contractors. Those erecting public buildings are pretty well up to date as a rule, it is to their interest to complete the building as quickly as possible, we keep back a percentage of the progress estimates, and I presume that has been the reason it has never been the rule in the Public Works Department to put in a penalty clause for the non-completion of a building. My hon. friend says it is customary in the case of private contracts. I do not know how it is in this part of the country, but in the province of New Brunswick I have known penalty clauses to be inserted, but I cannot call to mind a single case where the penalty has been exacted. It would never be exacted unless there had been unreasonable and unjustifiable delay on the part of the contractor. It is not worth wdiile putting anything in a contract that you are not going to enforce.
The minister says that there has been no public inconvenience from delay in completing a building. He makes that statement without any evidence whatever.
Except in rare instances, I say.

If he will look at the files of the department he will find that he is mistaken about this matter. A penalty clause for delay may not be enforced except under extraordinary circumstances, but at the same time the owner of the property, by having a penalty clause, has an argument or a club over the contractor to get him to finish his building when he agrees. This afternoon we had a discussion with regard to the Halifax public building, which was behind time, and it is an immense inconvenience to the public. I will recall to the minister's mind the Ottawa post office here, which was a scandal. None of us in this city could understand why it took such a long time to restore that building after it had been burned, and, therefore, I cannot agree with the minister. It seems to me that even if he does not enforce this penalty except under extraordinary circumstances it would be for the benefit of the public service, and I am sure that many instances could be given where the public has been inconvenienced from not having buildings completed in time. The post office in Ottawa was a special case in point and there never seemed 'to be any reason why it should be so.

My hon. friend suggests the best possible reason why a penalty should not be inserted. He says that it would not be exacted except under extraordinary circumstances. What a lever it would place in the hands of the minister to give him power to exact a penalty or not just as he pleased, if the contractor is behind time! You place a penalty clause of $25 a day in the contract and the minister can exact it as he pleases or may be the judge as to whether the circumstances were extraordinary or whether there was reasonable ground for the delay. My own idea is that whatever we put in a contract with the government shall be enforced under all circumstances and against everybody and that there shall be no lever left in the hands of the minister. If we put in a penalty clause we should enforce it. But it would be a very harsh thing to do. It might cause great hardship and be ruinous to contractors. We would have to put it in in the case of a small building as well as a large building. We would have to make the penalty commensurate with the size of the contract. If it were a large contract we would have to have a penalty of $25, $50 or $100 per day, in smaller contracts proportionately less, and in many cases to enforce it would simply mean ruin to the contractors. Notwithstanding the case to which the hon. gentleman has referred, I have since I have been minister, known very few instances in which the public have suffered any inconvenience by reason of delay in the completion of a contract.
What about the Halifax building?
That is one that my hon. friend referred to.

The minister makes an extraordinary argument. He says that he should not have anything in the contract but what he proposes to enforce. He brings in a contract for a public building at Campbellton which is to be finished next fall, and at the same time he practically tells the contractor that he can finish the building whenever he pleases, that there is no method of making him finish it at the time the contract calls for, that, in other words, the contractor can please himself as to when he will finish the public building, in the meantime the public can suffer and the minister has no power to enforce the contract.

Does the minister not appreciate that he can trust himself to use discretion in the matters that he has spoken of? Does he think that he could not trust himself to use discretion? The minister says that it would never do in all cases to exact the penalty. Supposing it was a glaring case, where a man 514
was not trying to finish his contract, either from taking advantage of the fact that the government might or might not exact the penalty, or was assuming that the government would not exact the penalty, would it not be a good thing in the interest of the public if the minister would exercise discretion as to having the penalty exacted? Could we not trust the minister to exact the penalty or to refrain from exacting it for a good cause, the onus always being on the man in default? It would seem to me that my hon. friend from Argente'uil (Mir. Perley) is quite right in saying that there should be a penalty clause. If the minister has that penalty clause he has it in his power, if it is a case where there is no excuse for the man delaying and therefore where morally as well as legally it should be exacted, to enforce it. But the converse is that when he has no penalty, because in some cases it might be harsh to enforce it, even when it is not harsh and^ its enforcement would be just and equitable, he is entirely remedyless. It is like a judge having no criminal code behind him to inflict punishment on somebody who has been proven guilty of a criminal offence. I cannot understand the hon. gentleman's argument that it would be doing anything wrong to have power to enforce a penalty unless it is that the hon. gentleman cannot trust himself to enforce it properly and equitably or to refrain from enforcing it.

Suppose that in the contract it was provided that for every day's default in the completion of a work the contractor should be liable to the Crown for a penalty of $25 per day, what right would I have as minister to give away that $25? What right would I have to exercise discretion?

The minister has the right which the existence of the Crown gives him, and the government do it every day. The government refrains from exercising rights every day against people, and they justify it by saying that there were peculiar and special circumstances why they did not enforce the rights of the Crcwn. Every day the right hon. gentleman and his government are not insisting against subjects upon things that technically they could insist upon. It is the prerogative of the Crown to say that it is not fair to a subject under certain circumstances to insist upon what it could legally exact. Could we not trust this government to say, the onus being upon the man who was in default technically, that the circumstances being such as to justify mercy, so to speak, we shall exercise our discretion and shall not insist upon a penalty? Surely the government could do that. That has

beer, going on practically every day since this government has been in power; it lias refiained from exercising the rights which it possessed. What about the Grand Trunk Pacific? Did we not have rights against the Grand Trunk Pacific that a year or two later we were told that it was not fair to enforce? We gave away some millions of the people's money because the govern-mnt said that it was not fair to hold them to the strict letter of the contract.
If I remember, the hon. gentleman did not approve of that?

I do not understand what the hon. gentleman means. _ I did not approve of this government doing things without a good excuse, and there was no good excuse for handing over that many mere millions of dollars to the Grand Tiunk Pacific. If there had been a good reason I would have been with the hon. gentleman in doing it. I am not saying that the hon. gentleman should do it where there is no good moral reason, but he is saying that even when there is good moral reason he should not have the power to enforce it. I say that he should have the power unless he has no faith in himself. The only answer is that he seems to believe that he would not be able to do justice to the people if he had that power. A lot of the other people think that is so, but I am astonished to^ find that the hon. gentleman puts himself in that position. I would think that while wo have responsible government, that government ought to be able to do justice as the circumstances warrant. They could determine whether it was a case in which the penalty should be enforced, the onus always being upon a person who was liable for the penalty to show good reason for not having it enforced against him. I cannot help but say that I think the reason for not putting in a penalty clause seems to be a deliberate refusal to protect the people of the country by having it in the power of the government to hurry on construction. Compare the progress made on the Chateau Laurier, in this city, with the progress made on the Museum, one built by a private corporation and the other by the government. Here we have exactly similar local conditions, but the Grand Trunk hotel has gone ahead ten times as fast as the Museum. Of course, there are no elections coming off, rnd the Grand Trunk can go ahead with its building and do business in a businesslike way, but the government has to delay for political exigencies.

The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that a penalty clause would not be effective unless it provided that the amount of the penalty should be regarded as liquidated damages. I apprehend that as a matter of law it would be Mr. LANCASTER.
the duty of the Minister of Public Works to deduct an amount as liquidated damages,
for every day's delay, from ths balance due on the contract.
Unless good cause were shown to the contrary.

If that were in the contract you might waive the penalty, but if it is in the contract that there shall be a penalty of say, $50 a day which shall be deemed liquidated damages no Minister of Public Works has the right to waive it, and it would be the duty of the minister to deduct that from the balance due on the contract. My hon. friend forgets that in respect to public buildings every contractor is obliged to have a security deposit for the completion of the contract. If there be any case of outrageous delay

which is the only case in which he says one ought to enforce a penalty-it is quite within the power of the minister to give notice to the contractor, take the work off his hands, let it to a new contractor and charge up against the security deposit and against apy balance due on progress estimates, what it may cost to complete the work. It has been found in the experience of the past, under the former government as well as this, that a penalty clause such as the hon. gentleman refers to is not necessary. There have been a very few instances since I have been minister in which the position of the public would have been in any way benefited by having a penalty clause.
If the work is not completed within the time mentioned in the contract is this deposit to be forfeited to the Crown?
If the minister takes the steps which the contract provides for by giving the contractor notice and taking the work off his hands, the minister has a right to look to the security cheque.
That is for the completion of the contract, but not for the delay.
Yes.

In the present contract
there is -a clause which gives the option to the minister to take the contract over and complete it, but at the same time he says he does not think it would be proper for him to insert a penalty clause which he could enforce if a contractor were abusing his privileges.

I said that I did not
think the minister should be free to exercise his judgment as to whether or not he should enforce a penalty clause. I said if it were made, as it ought to be made, in the nature of liquidated damages, it ought to be enforced in every case irrespective of

whether the contractor was a friend or a foe, or whether he was a strong man or a weak man.

The same argument whicli
applies to the deposit for non-completion of the contract should apply to penalty for delay to complete the contract within the stipulated time. What difference in principle is there between the two things. The minister can now exercise his option to take over the contract and that is a far more severe proceeding for the contractor than a penalty clause would be.

Leaving all these theoretical ideas aside does the minister not think that this is a very special case. In Campbellton all the buildings in the town were wiped out by fire, and since then the people must have been suffering great inconvenience in using a temporary post office. For that reason if for no other does not the minister think that special means should have been taken in this case to have the new post office speedily constructed, and no better means could be taken than those suggested by the hon. member for Argenteuil?	,

I am happy to say, from my knowledge of the contractor in this case, that I have not the slightest doubt but that this building will be completed in good time. My hon. friend need have no fear upon that point.

That is a very poor excuse. A great many of these contractors are very good men, but it is notorious that it takes longer to erect a government building than a building for a private party. The reason is that the contractor can practically finish a government building whenever he pleases. There is no penalty if he does not complete it within the stipulated time, and he does whatever best suits him. If a contractor is erecting a building for me, and another building for the government, and I am pressing him to complete he will devote his attention to my building simply because I will not stand for the delay, but the government will be satisfied and he can take as much time as he likes. This is a very special case, and it is very necessary that the people of Campbellton should have that public building completed immediately. I ask the minister now to put a penalty clause in the contract if the building is not completed in time.
I cannot make an exception in one special case, and besides the contract for this building has already been signed.

The matter becomes worse in view of the minister's last statement that he signed this contract before
getting the estimate before the House. He is very much afraid of putting >a clause in the contract that would be harsh to the contractor ; but he has very little respect apparently for the people of this country.
It was done under a Governor-General's warrant in accordance with the law.
And we are told that a certain condition cannot be put in now because the contract has been made.

What would have been the use of obtaining a Governor General's warrant to proceed as rapidly as possibly with the building if we waited until the Supply Bill passed, which would be in the latter part of next spring?

To get 'back to the hon. gentleman's statement, what would be the use of haste unless you did compel the contractor to hurry up the work and to pay a penalty if he did not hurry it up? According to the hon. gentleman's own statement, expedition was needed, and therefore a Governor General's warrant had to be got, and yet he is afraid to put in a penalty clause to compel the contractor to finish the work speedily. I think the hon. gentleman becomes more inconsistent every time he tries to justify this matter
I understand that none of the government buildings are insured, and therefore, I assume that this was a total loss to the government.
Yes.
Can the minister tell us how it happened that this building was burned?

The whole town of Campbellton was destroyed, only five or six buildings being left in the town limits.
Chatham public	building-enlargement,

This is to make a very necessary enlargement of the public building of Chatham. It is occupied for the post office, and also for the staff of the Public Works Department, the resident engineer of which resides at Chatham. They are very much cramped for room, and it is absolutely essential to make this addition. It is proposed to build an extension upon land which has been purchased. Two lots were purchased, one for $200, and the other for $2,800. It is estimated that the total cost will be $12,000.
What is the population of Chatham?
About 6,000, or possibly 7,000.
This estimate is to cover the entire cost of the building?
Yes.
No money has been spent up to date?

No, except to buy the land.
Fairville public building, $15,000.
What is that to cost?
My impression is aibont $25,000.
What is the population?
It is a manufacturing town. The population is about 3,500, including the villages surrounding, which for all practical purposes are a part of Fairville.
What is the revenue from the post office?
What county is it in?
The county of St. John, on the west side of t'he river.
Has the minister any rule in erecting these public buildings, as to the population, or the postal revenue of the town, and is the cost of the building proportionate to the size of the town?

To the last question I would answer yes. To the first I would say there is no settled rule as to population, hut we are not in the habit of erecting public buildings at places of less than from 1,500 to 3,000 people. There are very few places in which we erect public buildings where the population is less than 1,500. It is only in rare instances that we erect public buildings where the population does not greatly exceed that. In the shire town of a county a public building might be erected though the population was less than that. We do have regard to the population and the business being done, and the postal revenue also. In Fairville there are eight lumber .manufacturing mills employing, before the Cushing mill was closed, 980 men.
What is the customs?
There is no custom house at Fairville. The people do their customs business in the city of St. John.
When was this amount first voted?
Can the minister tell us what the revenue was then?
Does the minister think that a $25,000 building is necessary where the revenue amounts to only $1,800?
That depends on circumstances. Fairville is an important place, and I think it is not an unreasonable expenditure.
The employees of these lumber mills evidently post their letters in the city of St. John when the rev-nue is so small at Fairville.
I see that the money rders increased in one year by about $1,00, and the postal revenue increased somewhat too. It is a growing town.
Will the minister tell us why this building was not started before, if the money was voted two years ago?

The reason is that the chief architect has been very busy getting ready plans and specifications for other buildings, and I thought my constituents would forgive me if I allowed this building to wait.
Fredericton public building-Government share of cost of permanent pavement put down by municipal corporation on Queen and Car-leton streets, $1,816.98.
This is to pay the balance of the amount we agreed to pay the city of Fredericton for the granolithic pavement in front of the public building.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Does this include the roadway as well as the sidewalk?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We will send in a bill from our own town for a roadway in front of the public building.
Is it the policy of the Public Works Department to pay for the permanent pavements 'and sidewalks in front of the Dominion public buildings throughout the country?
It has been the practice to contribute a portion of the cost.
What proportion ?	r
Usually we provide half the cost of the frontage.
Is that course pursued in other cities?
Yes.
Is it followed in Toronto?
I do not know that Toronto has asked for it.
I suppose Toronto will be reimbursed in the same way as Halifax and these other places.
That does not follow. It will be time to consider that when .Toronto city makes any claim.
I am just putting a hypothetical case.
But I am not in the mood to-night for inviting municipalities to make claims against the government.

But the hon. gentleman forgets that we had a return of expenditures on these post offices brought down last year. The excuse given for the increase in the expenditures on the postal service was the number of post offices opened in the Northwest Territories, but when the return was brought down we were amazed to find that the post offices in Manitoba and the Northwest were all paying good dividends. The proportion of expenditure to revenue was as 90 to 100. Where the vast losses have occurred is in the eastern provinces. I do not wish to be provincial or narrow, but when the minister is distributing favours in the shape of post offices, he should consider those sections where the postal service gives a revenue over expenditure. As regards those pavements. I recollect the government refusing to pay anything for pavements in front of public buildings in Ontario.
My hon. friend is entirely mistaken. In the estimates of last year he will find some amount for that very purpose.
Would the hon. minister come down to particulars?

Take the case of Stratford, we paid a portion of the cost of paving there. Take the city of Ottawa, we agreed to pay what is called the local improvement tax, although under the British North America Act we are not legally bound.
That was the first time you did it.

I do not know, but there must always be a first time. My hon. friend will find that in other places, where the circumstances made the pav-ment a proper one, we did pay a portion of the cost of paving. I believe, however, that the old Conservative government refused to pay, and perhaps that is what my hon. friend has in mind. We, however, have adopted a different policy. I am of the opinion that, notwithstanding the provisions of the British North America Act, this government ought to pay its fair share of improvements in the way of granolithic pavements in front of its buildings.
In putting up a new building, the government always more or less damages the street in front.
Would I be unkind in calling attention to the fact that the hon. minister was a very devoted supporter of the old government to which he refers.

What has that to do with the action of this government? I am not finding fault with the old government. It was right under the British North America Act, but what I say is that we are proceeding on broader lines of equity, justice and fair play to the municipalities.
The old government, in many cases, was just as generous as my hon. friend's in that respect.
I was not blaming the old government.
The sum of $2,094 already paid was in part payment for this pavement.
Yes, and this is to provide for the balance.
That would make the government share of paving these streets about $4,800.

Yes. In Fredericton there is not only the post office and custom house, but the militia building and barracks, and this includes pavements for the frontage of all these different properties.
Grand Falls public buildings, $15,900.
What is this to cost?
The contract price is $17,777.
What is the population?

In 1901 it was 1,897, and
it must have increased since at least 50 per cent. Grand Fails is growing very well indeed. There is almost an absolute certainty that in the very near future an undertaking will be established by a company for the development of Grand Falls, which is perhaps the finest water-power next to Niagara. The company are to establish a pulp and paper mill with a capacity of 200 tons per day. Grand Falls is not only an important place to-day, but has apparently a splendid future.
What was the revenue?

$3,318 and the money orders $85,000.
Hampton public buildings, $3,000.

This is for the erection of a small building for a post office. Hampton is a shire town-an important village. The population in 1901 was over 2,000. The

intention is to put up a neat building which will cost probably $5,000.
What is the revenue?
It is not large. It was $660 and money orders $12,450.
In what county is it?
Kings County. It is the shire town.
Has the site been purchased?
Not yet. I have a little hope that possibly the railway department may furnish the site on a very pretty square opposite the railway station. If not we will buy a site in the immediate vicinity.

I have noticed that the minister frequently justifies the erection of these public buildings by saying that they are to be erected in shire towns. Are we to assume that his policy is to erect a post office in every county town ? And, if that is the rule for the province in which he lives, I ask the minister how he reconciles it with the fact that he does not apply that rule to other provinces.
For instance, what place?

I am not going to mention any particular place, for I am not asking the hon. gentleman for a post office-not necessarily, we are getting along fairly well, and I presume that if I did ask him to erect a post office in the county town of the county I represent, the Minister of Finance would come down later in the session and charge me with trying to increase the public expenditure. But the fact remains that the shire town of the county I represent is about three times the size of the town under discussion, is altogether an important town and has been a county town for upwards of fifty years.
May I ask the name of that town?

The hon. gentleman can guess it. He speculates a good deal, and I think he is a pretty good guesser. I have no doubt he has the name in his mind at this moment, and it is unnecessary for me to give it. But that is not the question: The question is, how does he reconcile the fact that every shire town in the province of New Brunswick is to have a public building, even though that town may be a place of only seven hundred people and with a small revenue, when he does not apply that rule in other provinces? I do not think he should give the fact of a town being a shire town as the reason for the erection of a post office there unless he is Mr. PUGSLEY.
prepared to follow the same rule in other provinces. I do not think it is a good reason. I will just wait a moment for the hon. minister's answer to my question.

My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) will doubtless remember that the Finance Minister, last session, or the session before, laid down what he thought, and what I feel sure his colleagues agree, would be a very safe rule to follow in these matters. He said it would not be unreasonable to erect one public building in a county where there was not absolutely good postal accommodation otherwise, and that a place which was a shire town other things being fairly equal, had the strongest claim to such public buildings. I entirely agree with the Minister of Finance, and I think I may say the same of all the members of the government. Let me say to the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) there are no two rules, the principle would apply to every county of Ontario, as well as of other provinces. Might I, while on my feet, without being too persistent, and without inviting any discourtesy from the hon. gentleman, ask him if he will tell me the name of the shire town of his county?
I think it is unnecessary.
I think it is Milton.
A pretty good guesser.

I may say, while I speak only for myself-and hitherto I did only speak for myself-that I feel that Milton had very strong claims for a public building. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) used formerly to rather advocate the claims of Milton. But I observe that to-night he intimates that Milton does not want a public building, that it is getting on pretty well and has sufficient postal accommodation. I should be sorry to consider a useless expenditure of public money in the town of Milton. But I was anxious to know if that was the town to which the hon. gentleman referred.

I do not wish the minister to go away with the idea that I made any statement to the effect that I would not like to see a post office erected in the town of Milton. But I have been asking for justice for that town ever since this government came into power, and I will not go on asking. I am not a beggar, and the county of Halton or the town of Milton dees not need that I should beg on its behalf. There is a fairly good post office building, rented by the government. But the people will be glad to have a public building erected, Understand, I am not begging the minister to do it, for I have been refused so often that my pride forbids me to repeat the request. But I can tell

th(- minister that the time will come when the town of Milton will get a public building, and it may not be so very far off either. I do not expect that the town will receive justice from the present ministry, at least so long as I represent the county. But I am going to represent the county as long as I think fit, and if he thinks he will punish the town and the county because the people choose to make me their representative, he can do so. I do not think he will compel the people to change their course by any such line of policy. Certainly, they have shown no sign of being influenced in that direction. But I must say the minister has not given a satisfactory answer to my question; he has not explained how it is that in one province a small town with a small revenue is given a public building and in another province a town three times as large, and a county town, is given no consideration at all.
Hartland public building, $15,000.
What is this building to coat?
The contract is for $16,700.
What is the population?
In 1904 it was 700. It is quite a rapidly growing town, and, though I do not know its present population, I suppose it would be in the vicinity of 1,000 or 1,200.
What is the postal revenue?
It is $1,955; money orders, $22,000.
Is this a shire town?
No. This building is intended to accommodate also the militia, affording a place for the storage of arms and equipment.

In what county is it?
Alr.^ PUGSLEY. Carleton. Hartland is a rapidly growing town, where considerable business is done.
Any customs?
No customs at present, but I think the building is intended for customs as well.
Is there any inland revenue?

Yes, there is inland revenue. The building is for post office and customs purposes and also for armoury accommodation for E Company of the 67th Regiment, Carleton Light Infantry. The contract price, $16,000, includes both heating and lighting. We have
adopted a plan which from remarks in the House I think will meet with approval, of letting contracts in such a way that they include heating and lighting.

Would the minister explain the principle underlying the erection of these buildings? In this instance Hampton has a population of 2,000 and a revenue of $660, and gets a $5,000 building. Hartland has a population of 700 and a revenue of $1,900 and gets a $16,000 building. If it is owing to the larger revenue that Hartland gets the more expensive building I can understand it. I realize that if people are businesslike and doing a great deal of business, 1,000 people may be using the post office and contributing to the revenue as much as 2,000 less progressive people in some other part of the country.

The circumstances in the two towns are a little different. While the population of Hampton is what is given here it is more scattered than the population of Hartland and the revenue is smaller. Then it may be that a considerable number of people having their homes at Hampton do their postal business at St. John, some 20 miles away. The people there are desirous of having a suitable post office but they will not require it for customs or inland revenue purposes, while the building at Hartland is to be used for that purpose and also as an armoury. Prominent citizens of Hampton represented to me that probably it would not be necessary to have caretaker's quarters in the building and that a one-story building with a basement, costing $5,000, would answer their purpose. At Hartland it is different. The revenue there is three times as great and, as I said, the building is for post office, inland revenue, customs and armoury purposes, all of which add to the cost. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) perhaps could give some further information on the subject.

I have no further information. I have no apology. to make for having asked the department to make a grant for a public building in Hartland. Instead of 700 I would say that the population is nearer 1,500. It is not incorporated for municipal purposes but is for fire and water purposes, and I presume the 700 refers to the fire incorporation, which is only the very centre of the town. It is the second largest town in the constituency and from a business standpoint it is very important. There are two large sawmills, a bank, a newspaper, and I suppose a dozen stores of all kinds. It is a live, hustling town and is entitled to what it is getting. I predict that in a few years the revenue will be twice what it

is. There are two companies of militia with headquarters at Hartland and both of these will be housed and quartered in the new building.
Is it intended to establish a drill shed as well as an armoury?
No, an armoury. The upper story is to be devoted to the two companies of the militia and the lower story to other public purposes.
Is there a public building in the county town?
Yes, in the town of Woodstock.
How far is it from Hartland?
Thirteen miles.
What is the size of the building? We can build a large building for $15,000 in our part of the country.

It is to have a frontage of 42 feet on Main street by a depth of 46 feet, two stories in brick with stone basement, basement floor concrete, basement partitions brick. Then there is a four story brick tower on the right anterior angle of the building.
What was the cost of the land for this building?
The minister says that a part of this building is an armoury on account of there being a company of a militia regiment there.
There are two companies, the member for Carleton says.

Has it been the custom to provide armouries where a company or two of a militia regiment is situated? I have a regiment in my county, a very good one too, and there is no provision of that sort for it. I would like to ask why it is that an armoury should be provided in a small village of this kind, whether it is the custom or whether the minister is making a precedent of it.

The necessity or desirability of doing this has been pressed upon my attention very strongly not only by some hon. gentlemen, but by the Militia Department. It is felt that if, in connection with public buildings, some suitable provision of a not very expensive character can be made for the accommodation of the militia in these smaller towns, it would be very desirable as giving encouragement to the militia and perhaps as saving the necessity which might exist in the near future of erecting separate buildings for armourv pur-Mr. CARVELL.
poses. I think it is a very good idea. It will certainly be a very great accommodation to the militia and it cannot add very much to the cost of the building.
Does the minister refer to the headquarters of a regiment or to where there is just a company or two?

I refer to a place just like this where there may be one or two companies. It is not at all undesirable in connection with a public building to add a little more space to give them some suitable place where their arms and equipment can be taken care of.
Who was the site purchased from?
It was purchased from a life long Conservative without any middleman being employed at all.
I think that we had better assume that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) knows more about this building than the minister.
I know all about this building. There were three Liberals who had sites that they wanted to sell, but they were not as suitable as the Conservative's site, and so the Conservative's site was bought.
Let us look into this.
There being a Conservative in this, the hon. gentleman thinks that he had better look into it.
Who carried on the negotiations for the purchase of this site?
We sent a representative of the department to examine the site- Mr. D. H. Waterbury, of St John.
Was the hon. member for Carleton with him?
No, I was not with him.
I may say that the fact that this site was bought from a Conservative is not to be attributed to the fact that Mr. Waterbury was appointed by the Conservative government.

My hon. friend knows how people change sometimes, having had some experience in that. But we are not debating the political side of it, we are trying to get at facts. When will this building be completed!
On the 19th February, 1912.
Have they commenced the work yet?
No, the contract was only let in November.
By competition?
Yes.
Where were the plans prepared?
In the department at Ottawa.
Who is the clerk of works?
Mr. Macfarlane. And, to give the hon. gentleman information which is not asked for, the wages are $3.50 per day not including Sundays.
How was he selected, and what were the qualifications?
I selected him.
Is he a builder?
He is a builder.
Since my hon. friend has furnished the politics-
He was recommended by a petition signed by all the prominent men of the town, both Liberal and Conservative.
Is that the way they select them now?
We do things honestly in Carleton county.
Does that price include the furnishing?
That includes the heating and lighting.

The cost, of the building will be approximately $3 per square foot of site, or $9 per square foot of ground area. It must be an exceedingly elaborate building. I do not think that this building here cost $9 per square foot of ground area.
Can my hon. friend suggest that you ever can get the cost of the building by taking the square area or the ground area?
My hon. friend knows that that is one of the roughest or quickest ways of calculating the cost of a building.
That is utterly absurd, you have to have the cubic contents, or the height of the building.

The minister forgets that I said that each floor would cost $3 per square foot of area.
Hillsborough public building, $15,000.
This is a revote,
Has the site been purchased from a Conservative?
No, this has been obtained from the Albert Manufacturing company.
What is the cost of the building? *
The estimated cost is $20,000. The plans have not been entirely completed yet, we have not called for tenders, but the instructions to the chief architect are to keep the cost to about $20,000.
What is the population?

By the census of 1901, it is 2,907. It is growing somewhat. It is a business centre where is located the Albert Manufacturing Company, a very large concern manufacturing gypsum and finding a market very largely in the United States, and here in the upper provinces.
The same people that you bought the site from?
They gave the site.
What is the reveue of the post office?
About $1,900. It is to be for the post office and custom house. It is an outport of Moncton. The custom duties were $11,612, money orders issued, $13,411, and money orders paid $7,197.
Were the plans prepared in Ottawa?
The plans are being prepared here by the chief architect.
When will this work be completed?
It is not under contract yet. We have not called for tenders.
When does my hon. friend expect to call for tenders?
In about a month or six weeks the plans and specifications, it is expected, will be ready.
How did the manufacturing company come to donate the site to the minister's department?

They are largely interested in the town, and having this land there, and being actuated, by public spirit, the officers of the company expressed a willingness to donate the site. It seemed the most suitable site which could be got.
It was suggested that the minister construct a wharf for them in return. Is there anything in that?
No, I do not think there is.
Did they construct one at the same place?
No, the hon. gentleman is thinking of Pink Rock.
You did it there?

No, not for the company.
Moncton armoury, $7,000.
This will not more than pay for the site. The representative of the Militia Department has recommended a very excellent lot of land in Moncton which we are proceeding to expropriate.
Is there to be a drill ground?
There is to be a parade ground.
What will be the total cost?
We have not yet had the plans prepared.
Why do you expropriate?

The hon. Mr. Emmerson, a member of this House, is executor of the estate of the late Mrs. Spurr and he did not feel it would be proper to make any agreement with him, and so the Exchequer Court will value the property.
Who selected the site?
Our own representative, and the representative of the Militia Department.
What procedure is taken to fix the price?

Usually we send an expert from the department to examine t'he available sites. We have at least one exceedingly good man in the department who has had large experience and he makes inquiry and reports. The Spurr estate has expressed a willingness to take $7,000 for this property which has a large area and is quite centrally situated, but we did not feel it would be proper to make an agreement with Mr. Emmerson, although he is simply the executor, having no interest in the property.
Who is the expert sent by the department?
Mr. Waterbury, of St. John, the superintendent of buildings for New. Brunswick.
What is the area?
I do not know exactly but the deputy tells me he thinks there are over two acres.

Property appears to be very dear in a town the size of Moncton. The last purchase we made there was at the rate of $23 per foot frontage.
Mr. PUGSLEY

The population of Moncton is now about 12,000. It was considered desirable to get a lot which would have railway connection for the accommodation of the artillery and we went a little bit out of the business centre and got quite a large area.

In Toronto, the Militia Department acquired a piece of land, held it for four years, and it is now being resold at a profit of $250,000. In the early days of Winnipeg a large tract of land was secured in the centre of the city, and it is now being sold at a very large profit by the government and land for military purposes is being acquired outside. I should think that the department should acquire a good sized tract of land here because there is no question but that Moncton will be a large city, and if the purchase is made at a reasonable figure the investment may become profitable some day. What troops will be accommodated in Moncton?

The 74th regiment called the New Brunswick rangers, and the 19th battery of artillery.
St. John drill hall, $100,000.

This is to supply a want which has been felt for a great many years. Fifteen years ago plans were prepared for a drill hall at St. John, but nothing was done. The site has now been obtained, and pursuant to a vote of last year tenders have been called, and we are about awarding a contract for the construction of a drill hall.
Has the land been purchased"?
Yes.

I understand there was an agreement with the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) who cannot possibly be in the House to-night, that one of the New Brunswick items should stand so that he may discuss these matters, and ask any questions he may think necessary. Will this item stand "for that purpose?
The understanding is that on any item he can ask a question and we have let the Lunenburg item stand.
Can my hon friend (Mr. Daniel) discuss these matters on items for Ontario or Quebec?
Yes I have no objection to that.
That arrangement will also apply to the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Crocket).

Certainly.
Tracadie Lazaretto, $5,000.
What is the policy of the government in regard to that?
Lepers are sent there for treatment and for care.
How is it progressing? Can the hon. gentleman give us any statistics about it?
I do not know of any cures being effected, but the patients are treated very kindly. I believe the nursing is done by the Sisters of Charity.
Is there an increase in the number of patients? I see a house is provided for in the vote.
That is for the medical superintendent.
The number of patients has been constant ever since I have been in office, varying from 18 to 23.
Are the accessions from foreigners?
One or two, but most of the patients are from the provinces down by the sea.	.
It is supposed that every leper in Canada is there?
Yes, except the Chinese in British Columbia, who are at D'Arcy Island, and these are returned to China.

It would facilitate the passage of these items if item 138 were allowed to stand, and those members who are absent were allowed to discuss any vote for public buildings in the maritime provinces on that item.
Mr. PUGSLiEY. I will agree to let item 138 stand, with the understanding that any member can discuss any maritime province building item when we take that up.
Lunenburg public building-improvements, $800.

I may say to my hon. friend from Peel that the chief architect has not been able yet to get the particulars with regard to the clock, but he will have them when we take up item 138. With regard to the electric wiring I find that tenders were called by public advertisement, and the time for receiving tenders will be up on the 18th instant, and the item of $800 is the estimate of the cost made by the chief architect.

With regard to the next item, ' Parrsboro public building, $15,000,' I believe this was passed this afternoon; but. with the permission of the committee, as I have only arrived in Ottawa to-night, I would like to ask if the plans have been prepared for that building?
No.
Are they in process of preparation?
No, they have not been reached yet.
Is it the intention of the minister to have them prepared at all soon?
Yes; that is the present intention, in the ordinary course, as soon as they can be reached, that plans and specifications will be prepared.
I take it that no tenders can be called for until those plans have been prepared?
No, they cannot.
Can the minister give me any idea when those plans in the ordinary course should be ready?

I am afraid to say, because there are a great many public buildings for which parliament has provided the mcney, and there are a large number for which the chief architect, with his limited staff, has not vet been able to prepare the plans and specifications. Therefore, it will be impossible for me to give my hon. friend definite information to-nigfit. All I can say is that in due course, when the chief architect reaches them, they will he attended to.

The answer of the minister is plausible, but not reasonable, inasmuch as a few moments ago an item was put through for a public building in the town of Hartland, N.B., and I think this is the first time we have had that item before us. In answer to my hon. friend from Peel, the minister informed the House, without the least hesitation, that tenders for that building were called by public advertisement in November, 1910, and that the building would be finished on the 19th of February, 1912. With respect to the Hillsborough public building, he says_ the plans have been prepared, and the building will be finished in a month or six weeks.
The Hartland item is not- a new item.
When did it appear before?
Last session.
Very good, that will not affect the purposes of my argument. In connection with the Parrsboro public building, how old is that vote?
That was some time ago and the plans are not ready.

But the minister said that the plans were in process of preparation and would be ready in a month or six weeks. That was the answer he gave and no doubt it was because the constituency was represented by a man behind him.
No, it was because the chief architect said the plans were in course of preparation.

That is the excuse the hon. minister gives now. This item is a hardy perennial. It made its first appearance in 1907-8, just preceding the last election, and was brought down the last days of the session. In reply to some observations from my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) the hon. minister then said:
I will not hold my hon. friend responsible for the amount of the expenditure, but under the authority of parliament I shall feel it my duty to proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of the building.
What year was that?

1907-8, volume seven of ' Hansard,' page 13327. That was just before the last general election. Coming down to last session, the same vote for the same building was under review again, and in reply to a question by the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) as to when tenders would be asked for, the minister said:
During the coming year, as soon as we get the plans ready.
As soon as we get the plans^ ready, you must take both together.

Certainly. He said tenders would be asked for during the coming year as soon as they got the plans ready. Now the minister has the audacity to come before this committee and say that the plans were not prepared because the department had a lot of other public works to attend to and each work must be taken in order. That answer is certainly evasive. It is not a proper or a correct answer. Contrast this with the expenditures in Hartland and Hillsborough. In these places the works were initiated last year. If the hon. gentleman does not propose to erect a public building in Parrsboro after buying a site for it, let him have the courage to say so and not tamper with the time of the House. In view of the attitude of the minister, I would be warranted, in justice to my constituents, in telling them that the Minister of Public Works is not serious when he says he intends to erect this public building, and that in all probability it will not be built.
I could not say anything else in view of the various statements made by the minister in' previous years.
What is the next item, Mr. Chairman?
My hon. friend from Cumberland has made a fair comment and I think is entitled to a reply.

But he does not leave me any chance to reply. He says he is Mr. RHODES.
I	" ~~

going down to give certain information to the people.
But we should have some specific assurance from the minister regarding his intentions.
I cannot prevent the hon. gentleman going down and talking to the people.
Does silence give consent?
Certainly I consent to his going down.

Then 1 take it from the minister that I can go and tell the citizens of Parrsborp which, to use his own words, is a very important and growing town with a population of over 3,000 and entitled to a suitable building for a post office, savings bank and custom house at an expenditure of $30,000-I can go and tell the people of Parrsboro, that, notwithstanding the statement of the Minister made four years ago, and his promise of last year, he only made these statements with the object of deceiving, or worse, the people of that locality. He authorizes me to say this because now he assures me that I can go and tell the people that he does not intend putting up this building.
I gave the hon. gentleman no such assurance. He did not ask my permission to go down to Cumberland.
Will the minister say that it is his intention to put up'this building?
I say it would be exceedingly foolish of my hon. friend to go to Cumberland and tell the people there anything of the kind he says he will.

In matters of policy, I have no doubt the minister would be a very apt guide to follow. I admit that as a question of political astuteness and perhaps from a political standpoint, I might be wrong in going to the people of Parrsboro and telling them that the minister does not propose to keep the word he gave on the floor of this House and is simply deceiving the public. But whether my experience in public life should happen to be long or short, I shall leave it _ with the consciousness that I have tried to act squarely, honourably and fairly, and have not twisted and squirmed and smiled at my friends in the rear, and made use of all sorts of cheap platform claptrap. If the minister does not propose to erect this building, let him say so, and not trifle with the committee by these sham statements.
When will the plans be ready?
I am not able to say because the chief architect is not able to tell me.
How is it that other items have been voted on for public buildings and passed long after this one, and the work commenced?
If my hon. friend had a great many things to do he would do them one by one and not attempt to do them all at once.
In rotation?
In rotation.

Why does the minister not follow that process here? This is one of the oldest items in the estimates. Surely the chief architect could have had these plans prepared inside of three years. He might have taken the blue prints of one of the other public buildings if necessary, unless he was told not to do so.
Let me say to the hon. gentleman that the minister and the chief architect must be the judges as to the order in which they will take up the preparation of plans for public buildings.
But a moment ago he said there were a great many public buildings to be erected.

There are a great many public buildings to be erected, and let me say that the town of Parrsboro' has no greater claim to a public building than the town of Hartland, and the hon. gentleman has no reason to complain. I have said very fairly that the chief architect is proceeding with the preparation of plans for the various public buildings and in due course he will reach this building. Let me say one word to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). The people of Parrsboro' will not suffer in any way by reason of the insinuations, [DOT]and what I think is the somewhat uncalled for conduct of the hon. gentleman. In dealing with Parrsboro' I shall recognize the claims of the people and not be influenced at all by the conduct of the gentleman who is representing them in this parliament.

The hon. minister has told us that the town of Parrsboro' has no more claim than the town of Hart-land. The vote for Parrsboro' was made long before that for the town of Hartland. The population of Parrsboro' is three or four times that of Hartland, and the postal revenue of the town of Parrsboro' is far greater than that of Hartland. In view of these facts will the minister not take back his statement that Parrsboro' is not better entitled to a public building than Hartland?
I cannot do so.
I suppose the minister will short-cut matters by saying that if he does not go on with the building this summer the deal is all off.
I have not said that.

It is pretty evident what the minister means to do, that is, to do on the eve of the next general election what he did on the eve of the last general election, and tell the people that they are going to get this building next year, when the plans are completed. The minister will not say that, according to his present ideas, he is not going to put up the building. I would not say anything as to delay so far as the chief architect is concerned, because I am sure he would have made these plans if he had not been told not to make them.
He would have had to neglect some other work.
But, according to my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), the minister stated two or three years ago that the plans would be got ready next year.
No. Well, perhaps, pretty nearly that.

Entirely that-next year, as soon as the plans could be got
ready.
He said that last year.

He said it back in 1907-8.
I will not hold my hon. friend responsible for the amount of the expenditure, but under the authority of parliament I shall feel it my duty to proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of the building.
Was he serious in making that statement? We must assume that he was. But the architect was not dismissed for disobedience of orders in not making the plans. There was no suggestion that he had been told, to make them and had refused, or that he had asked for help to make them and had been denied. The plans were not made, and no fault was found. Is it not manifest that the architect must have been told not to make them-for, since then, he has made plans for buildings in places of much less importance. There can be no other fair inference than that the making of these plans has been stopped, and that, for the present at all events, the minister does not intend to go on with the building. As an impartial judge, that is the conclusion I should come to. I live hundreds of miles away from Parrsboro' and these other places, and, as an impartial judge, I can come to no other conclusion than that the people * are being trifled with and misled. Whether

intentionally or not, they are being trifled with and misled.
Are you quite sure?

I am much sureT than the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) is about these matters. He has his own way of looking at these things, which is neither the people's way nor mine. But I was at out to say to the minister: If Parrsboro' is to be treated in this way, if a building is to be promised and that promise not carried out and yet the minister is not prepared to stand up manfully in this House and say that the building is not to be constructed, is it not plain that the minister's intention is to hold the matter open for another general election, when it is to be agitated again and the silly, worn out argument is to be used that the people must elect a supporter of the government or they will not get the building? This is the argument the Prime Minister had to repudiate when made by one of his ardent supporters in the west.
It was not made.
Was the hon. gentleman there?
Yes.
The hon. gentleman from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) wa3 there.
The hon. member for West Lambton was at a meeting where such a statement was not made?
Yes.
But the hon. gentleman will find in the newspapers on his own side of politics-I am speaking of the statement that
Never said it.
Then, why did the Prime Minister have to disagree with the gentleman who was alleged to have said it. and say that he had no authority for such a statement?
No, no.
The newspaper reporting the Prime Minister, represented the Prime Minister as saying that the statement was made indiscreetly-
Never made it.
But the people believe it was made, and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) by his action in regard to Parrsboro' encourages that belief.
No, no.

Yes, yes. By his actions, which speak louder than any words, no matter how smoothly he may utter them, though he speaks them with the greatest unction and the blandest of smiles, he convinces the people of the truth of this charge. When a general election was coming on, Parrsboro' was promised a public building next year as soon as the plans could be got ready. But the people did not see fit to elect the candidate the minister wanted them to elect, and the minister, instead of commending their independence and recognizing their right to exercise their franchise in their own way, instead of being big enough to go on with the building as promised, instead even of having the pluck to say that the building would not be constructed, takes up space in the estimates and takes up the time of this House in discussions as to whether this is to be built or not
I have not taken up one-fifth of the time taken up by hon. gentlemen opposite.

But the minister puts this item in his estimates and brings up the discussion in this chamber, and even until this minute he will not tell us whether this building is to go on or not. He, and he alone, is responsible for this discussion, if it should last for six weeks. We can understand that he wants the people to believe that he will give them this building when they elect a supporter of the government. But they probably are big enough to elect whom they please, and not accept this building if it is to be given as a bribe for their vote. If the people of that section are like the people of Ontario, the vote would be all the more in favour of my hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes) because they are subjected to this treatment by the government.

I desire to take advantage of the opportunity afforded by my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) retailing one of those slanders so often found in the Conservative press to refer to this question which, I understand, he introduces, relating to an alleged utterance of mine in Lethbridge. No such statement as is attributed to me was ever made by me.
I did not mention the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald).

But the hon. gentleman knows that certain of the press associated with his party have been retailing that stale slander for some time. The statement was contradicted immediately afterwards by the Lethbridge ' Herald ' and it was understood by the people in the vicinity that the statement attributed to

me had never been made. I took the first opportunity to contradict it when I returned to my own province. I have here a
press report of the referenced made to it:-

He paused to consider an article in the ' Herald ' of that city in which it was stated that Mr. Borden had got after him because of an alleged statement of his at Lethbridge. That fact did not worry him much. It was an evidence of the lack of any substantial criticism of the tour, when all Mr. Borden could find to talk about was an alleged statement which he had never made and its only foundation was a report in a party hack. What he had told the people of Lethbridge who wanted public buildings, was that Mr. Borden was campaigning in Nova Scotia and that the chief burden of his speeches was. the extravagance of the government; that Mr. Doherty, his new chief lieutenant, was especially strong in his condemnation of the building of post office buildings unnecessarily; that the Halifax ' Herald/ the organ of Mr. Borden, had in glaring headlines, declared that Sir Wilfrid Laurier could spend millions in the west but could not spend thousands in Halifax, and that if they followed the Conservative party on these lines they could never hope to get public buildings from the Conservatives. That was what he -said and he was prepared to stand by it. It was about time that Mr. Borden gave up preaching his homilies, usually based on incorrect facts, and got to work to find out a policy for his party.
That is a correct statement of what I said at Lethbridge and I never made the statement that the people of Lethbridge or any other place in Canada would never get public buildings so long as they voted Conservative. I desire to make that statement because this is a report which has been bandied about in every nondescript Conservative paper in the country.

It is certainly not the first opportunity that has been taken because the Prime Minister took a very much earlier opportunity to correct the hon. gentleman and it was so stated in some newspapers that the Prime Minister, only a few days after, had stated that the hon. member who has just spoken had been ill-advised in the statements he had made, or words to that effect. The Minister of Public Works brings this matter up by his action in regard to the Parrsboro' building. If I had the time I could find for my hon. friend in the library-

Does my hon. friend in the face of the absolute contradiction I have given to that statement undertake to argue that the statement was made ? Because if he does, I want to state that the statement attributed to the Prime Minister is absolutely untrue.

The hon. gentleman must not ask me to take his denials wholesale in regard to everybody. He confines 52
his denial to what the leader of the opposition says.
Not at all.
Yes, bringing in a supposed speech of the leader of the opposition who, I suppose was Mr. Borden.
That is what I said.
The hon. gentleman got up to tell us what he had said in a crit icism of Mr. Borden's speech, when he had said off his own bat in Lethbridge-
The hon. gentleman has given what he said.

He has given what he said afterwards or his construction of what he said. I can show the hon. gentle man the statement in important papers, reporting the Prime Minister's statement within a few days afterwards correcting the impression made by the hon. gentleman who has just sat down. When his own Prime Minister saw fit to correct him within a few days the hon. gentleman must allow us to assume that the Prime Minister had some- reason for correcting him.

My hon. friend from Sarnia (Mr. Pardee) with myself accompanied the Prime Minister all through that tour. The Prime Minister did not at any of the meetings, and we were present at them all, make such a statement as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has attributed to him, and I never saw in any paper any such statement attributed to the Prime Minister at any time after the tour and no such speech was made during the tour.

I do not propose to be tied up to speeches made at public meetings. The Prime Minister, in a newspaper, it may have been in an interview with a newspaper reporter long before the session commenced, corrected the impression taken by the country from the hon. member's speech at Lethbridge. If the Prime Minister found it necessary to correct that impression, let the hon. member fight it out with the Prime Minister and not find fault with us for referring to it.
Has the Minister of Public Works ever instructed the chief .architect to prepare plans for the Parrsboro' post office?

The chief architect receives general instructions to proceed with the preparation of plans for the different public buildings for which parliament had granted appropriations. I gave no special instructions with regard to Parrsboro' one way or the other.
Did he give any special instructions with respect to the Hartland public buildings or anything more than the general instructions to prepare plans?
I do not recall to mind giving any special instructions as to the Hartland building.
I would like to have the minister look into the matter a little further and recall it to mind, if not to-night, subsequently, and let us have the information.
As to what?

As to whether the chief architect of his department had received any instructions to prepare plans for the Hartland public building other than the general instructions which would include instructions to prepare plans for the Parrsboro' post office?
If my hon. friend makes a motion in the House to that effect I would be very glad to furnish a return showing any instructions given as to the Hartland building or the Parrsboro' building.
Am I to understand that in order to get the information I must move for a return?
It is better and more regular.

I will quote the statement of the minister as reported at page 13327 of ' Hansard ' of the session of 1907-8. He said : I
I shall feel it my duty to proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of the building.
Does the minister feel that he has complied with these words ; that he has proceeded as rapidly as possible with the construction of this building, that is bearing in mind the fact that- these remarks were uttered on July 16, 1908?

The non. gentleman must take in connection with that my statement that as soon as plans are prepared the instructions were issued to call for tenders. I can say yes to my hon. friend, unless I had gone outside and selected some outside architect to do the work. I have been pressed by different members to proceed with the erection of certain buildings and have been obliged to go out and get outside architectural assistance because the chief architect was not able to undertake the work. There has been too much work to do. Some of the staff have been sick, two or three of them were laid off during a considerable part of toe summer, and it is a fact that for a great many public buildings to be built, some of them in constituencies represented by Mr. PUGSTjRy.
government supporters in the House, including my own constituency of the city and county of St. John, the chief architect has not yet been able to prepare plans. Let me say that I am not going, simply because the hon. member gets up in the House and blames me for treating Parrs-borro' wrongly, because he has induced my hon. friend now in my eye to get up and say that I am holding up that

You are misquoting me,. I never said you were treating Parrsboro' wrongly. I said you were .treating the House, the committee, and the public life of this country wrongfully. Parrsboro' will take care of itself.

The hon. gentleman will not, by expressions or comment like this,, induce me to treat Parrsborough any better than any other constituencies in this country are being treated, or constituencies which have elected supporters of this government to parliament. I referred to-night to my own constituency, a constituency which has been faithful to me and a community where I received a very large majority of votes. A portion of that constituency-Fairville- was almost unanimous in my support, and although there was an appropriation two years ago for a building, the chief architect has not reached it. I do not think he has done one single thing towards the preparation of the plans simply because he has been rushed and unduly pressed with work in connection with this department. I am not going to ask him to take up Parrsborough and to give it precedence over other buildings.
I am not asking that.

I should not think of doing it. When the chief architect, in due course, reaches Parrsboro', I take it for granted that, in accordance -with the vote of parliament, he will prepare the plans. I have no intention not to go on with this work of erecting a public building in Parrsboro, but I am not going to be hurried by anything my hon. friend may say. I am not going to be hurried by any threat that he is going to tell the people that I am treating Parrsboro' unfairly.
I never said that.

I am going to let the matter take its course and when, in the ordinary course, the chief architect reaches Parrsboro' and prepares the pllans and specifications, I presume that my colleagues will agree that the contract shall be let and the work proceeded with. When I made the statement last year I made it in good faith. I do not think that the hon. gentleman at all helps the case of his constituency by insinuating that I was not acting in good faith, or that his colleague, who was associated with him, and w'ho is just now
163?

leaving the House, helps the case when he says that I have been acting in bad faith and that I have no intention of acting upon the vote of parliament. I repeat that in due course, when the chief architect reaches the proposed building and prepares the plans and specifications, I have no reason to doubt that the department, having received the approval of the government, will take the necessary steps for the erection of a building.
Then we may expect. the plans on the eve of the next election?
