I would like to ask the minister if he ever gives any other instructions to the department of the chief architect but the general instruction to prepare plans for these buildings, the names of which appear in the estimates? Does he ever say to the chief architect: Will you kindly hasten the plans of such and such a building?
Yes.
Then, may I ask the minister if he is putting Parrsboro' on the same basis as other places? Did he ever knew of a work having received a preference?

There are cases where a member would say to me that there is the very greatest possible necessity for a public building in such a place, the accommodation is very poor, the post office is wretchedly situated, and urging that we shall go ahead. In cases of that kind I send a memorandum to the chief architect asking him how the plans are progressing and asking thaf the plans shall be prepared with as little delay as possible. I do not remember that I have had my attention called to the very urgent, immediate necessity for the erection of a building in Parrsboro'.
Why was the land purchased three years ago?

It was purchased under the authority of parliament because it was reported to the department that a public building was required. But what I mean to say is that in some places there may be a greater necessity for a public building than in other places.
Port Arthur is one of these places.
Probably Port Arthur.
Sudbury.
Lethbridge.

Lethbridge, too, in a constituency represented by an hon. gentleman on the othCT side of the House. I think the case there is urgent. I intend to press that forward with a little more haste 52*
than I would employ towards public buildings in some other places, because the conditions are such as would require urgency. A3 soon as parliament passes the appropriation I will instruct the chief architect to have that building proceeded with, even though some other building may be delayed, and even although we may have to delay for a little while longer the preparation of the plans for Parrsboro'.
Is that the post office that was promised by the Prime Minister in his tcur?
Yes.
That is the one that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said they would not get unless they stopped voting Tory.

The hon. member for Pictou did not say that, and I am surprised that an hon. gentleman so far forgets the duty which he owes to this House and to hon. members as to repeat that statement after the denial of the hon. member.

The hon. gentleman knows very well that an hon. member of this House can rise in his place and deny things. I have had a certain case-I do not wish to bring it up here-where a minister of the Crown rose last session on the floor of this House and said
Order, Mr. Chairman.
All right.

In my previous reference to Parrsborough, I was careful to quote the exact words of the minister, to ask certain1 questions and to make certain observations after having done so. I refrained from speaking of the case of Parrsboro', but I propose to do so now. I may say to the minister that the case of Parrsboro' is urgent. They are very poorly served with the most inferior wooden building which is entirely inadequate to the service of a town of that size. It is upon a back street in a very unsuitable portion of the town. If a building were constructed upon the lot which was purchased by the government it would be unquestionably in, if not the most favourable situation, certainly in as good a location as could be obtained in that part of the town. It is very near the railway station and upon the Main street. The business men of Parrsboro' really require a much better post office service than they have at the present time. Parrsboro' is a much more important town than even the population would indicate although it is much larger than many towns now served by post offices because it is a shipping port, and in the summer time there is a great deal of business done. There are many large interests served there, the representatives of which use the post office, and are interfered with by reason of the location of the post office in the town. I do not

think the minister was quite fair in the answer to the question I put to him a moment ago after quoting his words wherein he said that he proposed to proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of the building. I asked him if he had carried out his intention in that respect, and he said that coupled with that was the statement made at the same time that as soon as the plans were prepared he proposed to go ahead. But, that promise was made in the year 1907-8. The remark which he proposed to couple with that was made during last year, ox only one year ago when he said: I propose to call for tenders this year, or as soon as the plans are prepared. There were, two years separating the two remarks, and I leave it to the fairness of the committee, if, in view of the fact that plans have been prepared for much smaller places and tenders never having been called for last year, his promise is carried out to proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of the Parrsboro' post office. This work was projected two years before some of the items referred to io-night and the minister stated that plans in one case had been prepared and that in the other they were in process of preparation and would be completed within one month or six weeks.
